m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Check that your computer can run the Unity 6 Editor.
  • Install Unity Hub, activate a free Unity Personal license, and install Unity 6.3 LTS.
  • Install a C# editor and tell Unity to use it.
  • Recognize and fix the install problems beginners hit most often.

Hollow Knight, Cuphead, and Among Us were all made in Unity. The Editor their teams used is the same one you are about to install, and for students it costs nothing.

Unity arrives in two pieces. Unity Hub is a small launcher that downloads Editors, opens projects, and holds your license. The Unity Editor is the multi-gigabyte program where you build games. You install the Hub once; the Hub then installs Editor versions side by side. That matters because every Unity project is tied to one Editor version, and opening it in a different one can trigger an upgrade you didn't plan for.

This course uses Unity 6.3 LTS (version numbers that start with 6000.3). LTS means Long Term Support: Unity fixes bugs in it for two years without changing how things work. If the Hub offers a newer Unity 6 LTS by the time you read this, that's fine too. Every script in the course uses APIs that exist across Unity 6.

#Can your computer run it?

Windows macOS Linux
System Windows 10 (21H1 or newer, 64-bit) or Windows 11 macOS 13 Ventura or newer Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04
Processor 64-bit Intel or AMD, or Arm64 on Windows 11 Apple silicon (M1 or newer) or Intel 64-bit Intel or AMD
Graphics DirectX 11/12 or Vulkan capable Metal capable (every Mac that runs Ventura) OpenGL 3.2+ or Vulkan, with NVIDIA or AMD drivers

Unity recommends at least 8 GB of RAM. Plan for roughly 15 GB of free disk space: the Editor itself takes several gigabytes, and each project grows a Library folder of cache files that can pass a gigabyte.

⚠️ Chromebooks can't run the Editor

Unity supports the Editor only on real Windows, macOS, and Ubuntu machines, not inside an emulator or container, and ChromeOS's Linux environment is a container. If a Chromebook is your only computer, ask your school or public library for time on a Windows PC or Mac. You can still read every lesson and write the C# files; you just can't press Play until you're on a supported machine.

#The free license, and who can sign up

Unity Personal is the free plan. It's for individuals and small groups with less than $200,000 USD of revenue and funding in the last 12 months, which covers every student project. You need a free Unity account to use it.

Unity's terms say you must be old enough to consent to the use of your personal data where you live: 13 in the US, 16 in much of the EU. If you're younger than that, a parent, guardian, or teacher should create the account and sign in for you.

#Step 1: Install Unity Hub

Windows

  1. Go to unity.com/download. The site asks you to sign in or create a free Unity account before it shows the download links.
  2. Download the Windows version of Unity Hub and open the file.
  3. Follow the setup window. Recent versions of the Hub (4.0 and later) install as a Windows app package, so there's no folder to choose.
  4. Open Unity Hub from the Start menu. If Windows Firewall asks whether the Hub can use the network, allow it; the Hub needs the internet to download Editors.

macOS

  1. Go to unity.com/download. The site asks you to sign in or create a free Unity account before it shows the download links.
  2. Download the macOS version of Unity Hub.
  3. Open the downloaded .dmg file and drag Unity Hub into Applications.
  4. Open Unity Hub from Applications. If macOS offers to install Rosetta, accept: Unity lists Rosetta 2 as a requirement on Apple silicon Macs.

Linux (Ubuntu)

Unity publishes the Hub as an apt package. Open a terminal and run these commands one block at a time (they're copied from Unity's install page):

Then open Unity Hub from your applications menu.

#Step 2: Sign in and activate Unity Personal

Open the Hub and sign in with your Unity account (or choose Create account). For Unity Personal, signing in normally activates the license by itself.

To check, click the Settings (gear) icon and open Licenses. If no license is listed:

  1. Click Add license.
  2. Choose Get a free personal license.
  3. Read the terms and click Agree and get personal edition license.

#Step 3: Install the Unity 6.3 LTS Editor

  1. In the Hub's left sidebar, click Installs.
  2. Click Install Editor (top right). The Official releases tab lists the LTS versions.
  3. Find the newest version that starts with 6000.3 and click Install.
  4. A list of optional modules appears. Tick only what you need:
    • Microsoft Visual Studio Community (Windows only): tick it if you want Visual Studio as your code editor. Skip it if you'll use VS Code.
    • Web Build Support: optional. It lets you export a version of your game that runs in a browser, which is handy for sharing it later.
    • Documentation: optional. It installs the manual for offline reading.
  5. Click Install and watch progress in the Hub's Downloads panel. Expect 10 to 40 minutes, depending on your connection.

You can add modules later: Installs, then Manage next to the version, then Manage modules.

#Step 4: Pick a C# editor and connect it

Unity scripts are C# files. You write them in a separate code editor, and Unity compiles them when you switch back to it. Either option below is free.

Windows

  • Visual Studio Community is the smoothest choice. If you ticked its module in Step 3, the Hub installed it for you. Either way, open the Visual Studio Installer, choose Modify, and make sure the Game development with Unity workload is ticked.
  • VS Code also works. Install it from code.visualstudio.com, open the Extensions view, and install Unity (published by Microsoft). It installs the C# extensions it needs on its own.

macOS

  • Use VS Code. Microsoft retired Visual Studio for Mac in 2024, so it's no longer an option.
  • Install VS Code from code.visualstudio.com, open the Extensions view (⌘⇧X), and install Unity by Microsoft. It brings the C# Dev Kit with it.

Linux (Ubuntu)

  • Use VS Code. Install the .deb package from code.visualstudio.com, then install the Unity extension by Microsoft from the Extensions view.

You'll point Unity at your editor in the next lesson, once a project is open: Edit > Preferences > External Tools (on macOS, Unity > Settings > External Tools), then set External Script Editor.

#What success looks like

The Hub's Installs page shows a version starting with 6000.3, tagged LTS, with no warning icon. Under Settings > Licenses you see an active Unity Personal license. That's everything; the next lesson creates a project and runs your first script.

#Fixes for the problems people actually hit

  • The download stalls or ends with "Validation failed." Usually it's a full disk or an interrupted connection. Free up space, pause antivirus scanning for the download folder if you're allowed to, and click Install again; the Hub resumes from what it already has.
  • "No valid Unity Editor license found." The Hub signed you in but didn't activate Personal. Use Settings > Licenses > Add license > Get a free personal license. If it still fails, sign out of the Hub, sign back in, and try again.
  • School or work computer refuses to install. Installing an Editor may need administrator rights. Ask whoever manages the computer, or check the Hub's Settings for the Editor install location and choose a folder inside your own user account.
  • Linux: apt can't find unityhub. One of the first two command blocks failed silently. Check that /etc/apt/keyrings/unityhub.gpg exists and that /etc/apt/sources.list.d/unityhub.sources contains the five lines above, then run sudo apt update again.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your friend's project was made in Unity 6000.3. You have 6000.0 installed. What's the safest move?

  • Opening a project in an older Editor than the one that made it can fail or break assets.

  • The Hub keeps Editor versions side by side, so matching the project's version avoids surprise upgrades or downgrades.

  • The Hub isn't the problem; it can hold several Editors at once.

Show answer

B. The Hub keeps Editor versions side by side, so matching the project's version avoids surprise upgrades or downgrades.

2You're on a Mac and want a code editor for Unity scripts. Which fits?

  • Microsoft retired it in 2024.

  • It's free, supported on macOS, and the extension adds Unity-aware autocomplete and debugging.

  • Unity will compile the file, but without the C# tooling you lose error highlighting and autocomplete for Unity's APIs.

Show answer

B. It's free, supported on macOS, and the extension adds Unity-aware autocomplete and debugging.

3Which part of the install needs the most disk space over time?

  • The Hub is small; it's a launcher.

  • Script files are tiny text files.

  • The Editor takes several gigabytes, and every project rebuilds a large Library folder of cached assets.

Show answer

C. The Editor takes several gigabytes, and every project rebuilds a large Library folder of cached assets.

Key takeaways

  • Unity Hub installs and launches Editors; the Editor is where you build. Each project belongs to one Editor version.
  • This course uses Unity 6.3 LTS (6000.3) with a free Unity Personal license.
  • Windows users can use Visual Studio Community or VS Code; macOS and Linux users should use VS Code with the Unity extension.
  • Chromebooks can't run the Editor, so plan for access to a Windows, Mac, or Ubuntu computer.

#Further reading

  • Install the Unity Hub (opens in a new tab): Unity's own steps for each operating system, kept up to date as the Hub changes.
  • Unity 6.3 system requirements (opens in a new tab): the full hardware and OS list, including graphics driver notes for Linux.
  • Unity development with VS Code (opens in a new tab): how the Unity extension works and how to debug a running game from VS Code.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a project from the Universal 2D template in Unity Hub.
  • Name the job of the Scene view, Game view, Hierarchy, Project, Inspector, and Console.
  • Confirm the project uses the Input System package, which every script in this course relies on.
  • Write, attach, and run a C# script that moves a sprite and reacts to the keyboard.

By the end of this lesson a white square will spin on screen, reverse when you press Space, and print a line you wrote into the Console. That sounds small, but it exercises every link in the chain: the Hub opens the Editor, the Editor opens your code editor, Unity compiles your C#, and Play mode runs it. If all of that works, nothing in later modules will be blocked by setup.

#Step 1: Create the project

  1. In Unity Hub, click Projects, then New project.
  2. At the top, check that the Editor version is your 6000.3 LTS install.
  3. In the template list, pick Universal 2D (it's in the Core group). If it shows a download button, click Download template and wait.
  4. Set Project name to UnityPlatformer and choose a Location you'll remember, such as a GameDev folder in your Documents.
  5. Leave any cloud or source control options off for now. Lesson 3 sets up backups your way.
  6. Click Create project.

The first launch takes a few minutes because Unity imports the template's packages and builds the Library cache. Later launches are much faster.

The Universal 2D template sets up the Universal Render Pipeline with its 2D renderer and installs the 2D packages (sprites, tilemaps, 2D animation). The starting scene, SampleScene, holds just two objects: a Main Camera and a Global Light 2D that lights your sprites.

#Step 2: Learn the six windows

Unity's layout can be rearranged, but the default has these six areas. You'll use all of them in every module.

Window What it shows What you do there
Hierarchy Every GameObject in the open scene, as a tree Select, rename, parent, and create objects
Scene view The scene from an editing camera Place and arrange objects
Game view What the Main Camera sees, which is what players will see Watch and play the game in Play mode
Inspector The components of whatever is selected Change values like position, color, speed
Project Every file in your Assets folder Make and organize scripts, sprites, prefabs, scenes
Console Messages, warnings, and errors Read Debug.Log output and fix errors

A few controls to try right now in the Scene view:

  • Scroll to zoom. Hold the middle mouse button and drag to pan, or press Q for the Hand tool and drag.
  • Select an object and press F to frame it.
  • W, E, R, and T switch to the Move, Rotate, Scale, and Rect tools.
  • The 2D button in the Scene view's toolbar should be on. It locks the view to face the XY plane, which is where a 2D game lives.

The Play, Pause, and Step buttons sit at the top center of the Editor. Play starts the game inside the Editor, and pressing it again stops.

#Step 3: Check the Input System and your code editor

New Unity 6 projects include the Input System package, Unity's current way of reading keyboards, mice, and gamepads. This course reads devices directly with code like Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame, which keeps every script short and readable. Two quick checks:

  1. Open Edit > Project Settings > Player, expand Other Settings, and find Active Input Handling. It should say Input System Package (New) or Both. If it says Input Manager (Old), switch it to Input System Package (New) and let Unity restart.
  2. Open Window > Package Management > Package Manager (in Unity 6.0 it's Window > Package Manager). Click In Project and confirm Input System is listed.

You'll see an InputSystem_Actions asset in your Project window. That's the template's ready-made action map, used by a different style of input code. We won't need it, but leave it in place.

Now connect your code editor: Edit > Preferences > External Tools (macOS: Unity > Settings > External Tools), and set External Script Editor to Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code. If you use VS Code, also check the Package Manager list for Visual Studio Editor at version 2.0.20 or newer; it's the package that links Unity to both editors.

#Step 4: Make a sprite and a script

  1. In the menu, choose GameObject > 2D Object > Sprites > Square. A white square appears in the scene.
  2. In the Hierarchy, rename it SpinTest (select it and press F2, or Return on macOS).
  3. In the Project window, right-click the Assets folder and choose Create > Scripting > MonoBehaviour Script.
  4. Type the name SpinTest immediately, before clicking anywhere else, and press Enter.
  5. Double-click the script to open it in your code editor. Replace everything with:

Save the file and switch back to Unity. A small spinner in the bottom-right corner means Unity is compiling.

Now attach the script: drag SpinTest.cs from the Project window onto the SpinTest object in the Hierarchy. Select the object and you'll see a Spin Test (Script) component in the Inspector, with a Degrees Per Second field showing 90.

#Step 5: Press Play and prove it works

Press Play. The square turns a quarter-circle every second. Click inside the Game view so it has keyboard focus, then press Space a few times. Open the Console tab (or Window > General > Console) and you should see:

Three lines in this script are worth a second look. Start ran once, before the first frame, which is why its message appears first and only once. Update runs every frame, and multiplying by Time.deltaTime (the seconds since the last frame) makes the speed "90 degrees per second" on any computer, whatever its frame rate. And wasPressedThisFrame is true only on the single frame the key goes down, so holding Space reverses once, not sixty times a second.

🧪 Try it yourself

While the game is still playing, change Degrees Per Second in the Inspector to 720. The square whirls. Now press Play again to stop: the value snaps back to 90. Changes made in Play mode are temporary, and Lesson 3 shows how to keep them when you want to.

#When it doesn't work

⚠️ "Can't add script component 'SpinTest' because the script class cannot be found"

The full message continues: "Make sure that there are no compile errors and that the file name and class name match." You renamed the file after Unity created it, so the file says SpinTest.cs but the code still says public class NewMonoBehaviourScript. Make the class name and file name identical, including capital letters, and save.

⚠️ error CS0103: The name 'Keyboard' does not exist in the current context

The using UnityEngine.InputSystem; line is missing or misspelled. Every script that reads Keyboard.current or Mouse.current needs it at the top. Until all compile errors are fixed, pressing Play shows "All compiler errors have to be fixed before you can enter playmode!"

  • Space does nothing, but there are no errors. The Game view doesn't have focus. Click inside it once while playing.
  • No autocomplete in VS Code. Set the External Script Editor as in Step 3, then in Unity choose Assets > Open C# Project so VS Code opens the whole project rather than a single file.
  • The square isn't visible in the Game view. It's outside the camera's view. Select it and set its Position to 0, 0, 0 in the Inspector.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You press Play, set a value in the Inspector, then stop. What happens to the value?

  • Play mode runs on a temporary copy of the scene; edits there aren't kept.

  • Unity restores the scene when Play mode ends, so the change is lost.

  • The Inspector never rewrites your C# source code.

Show answer

B. Unity restores the scene when Play mode ends, so the change is lost.

2Which window would you use to change the color of the selected square?

  • The Project window lists files; it doesn't edit the object's components.

  • The Hierarchy selects and organizes objects, but values live in components.

  • The Sprite Renderer component, shown in the Inspector, has the Color field.

Show answer

C. The Sprite Renderer component, shown in the Inspector, has the Color field.

3If you hold Space down for two seconds, how many times does the spin reverse?

  • wasPressedThisFrame is true only on the frame the key goes down.

  • That's what isPressed would do, since it stays true every frame the key is held.

  • The press is detected on its first frame.

Show answer

A. wasPressedThisFrame is true only on the frame the key goes down.

Key takeaways

  • The Universal 2D template gives you a URP 2D project with a camera, a 2D light, and the 2D packages.
  • Hierarchy = objects in the scene, Inspector = the selected object's components, Project = files, Console = messages.
  • This course reads input with Keyboard.current and Mouse.current from UnityEngine.InputSystem.
  • A script's file name and class name must match, and changes made during Play mode are thrown away when you stop.

#Further reading

  • Creating scripts (opens in a new tab): the official steps for making MonoBehaviour scripts, and the other script types in the Create menu.
  • Input System: Keyboard support (opens in a new tab): how Keyboard.current and each key control work, including the difference between isPressed and wasPressedThisFrame.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Tell the difference between saving a scene, saving a script, and changes that vanish when Play mode ends.
  • Organize Assets so files are easy to find, and move them without breaking references.
  • Back up a project with Git and a Unity .gitignore, or with a zip that skips the cache.
  • Read Console errors, find the line that caused them, and use a repeatable routine to fix them.
  • Set up the Editor so it's comfortable to use, and keep yourself and your players safe.

You spend twenty minutes in Play mode tuning a jump until it feels perfect. You press Play to stop, and every number snaps back to the old values. Almost every Unity developer does this once. This lesson is about the habits that keep it from happening twice, plus the routine for when something breaks.

#Three kinds of "saved"

Unity has more than one thing to save, and each works differently.

  • Scenes are saved from Unity: File > Save (Ctrl+S, or ⌘S on macOS). An asterisk after the scene name in the Hierarchy means it has unsaved changes.
  • Scripts are saved in your code editor. When you switch back to Unity, it notices the change and recompiles.
  • Play mode changes aren't saved anywhere. Unity restores the scene when you stop.

To keep a value you found during Play mode, right-click the component's title bar in the Inspector and copy the component. Stop playing, right-click the same title bar, and paste the component values. Every field you tuned comes back.

💡 Make Play mode impossible to miss

Open Edit > Preferences > Colors (macOS: Unity > Settings > Colors) and set Playmode tint to a strong color. The whole Editor turns that color while the game runs, so you'll notice before you start a long edit.

#What's inside a project folder

Open your project folder in File Explorer or Finder. Only some of it is yours.

Folder What it holds Back it up?
Assets Your scenes, scripts, sprites, prefabs, sounds Yes
Packages The list of packages the project uses (manifest.json) Yes
ProjectSettings Input, physics, tags, layers, and player settings Yes
Library Unity's cache of imported assets No, Unity rebuilds it
Temp, Logs, UserSettings Scratch files and your personal Editor layout No

Deleting Library while Unity is closed is a safe fix when a project acts strangely after an update. The next launch takes longer while Unity rebuilds it.

Inside Assets, make a folder for each kind of thing. Right-click in the Project window and choose Create > Folder:

⚠️ Move files inside Unity, not in File Explorer or Finder

Every asset has a .meta file beside it that holds its unique ID. Scenes and prefabs refer to assets by that ID, not by name. If you move Player.png in Finder without its .meta file, Unity makes a new ID and every object that used the sprite shows Missing. Drag files between folders in Unity's Project window and the .meta files move with them.

#Back up with Git (or a zip)

Git keeps a history of your project, so a bad change can be undone in seconds. New Unity 6 projects already use the two settings Git needs, visible .meta files and scenes saved as text, so there's nothing to change.

The key file is .gitignore, which tells Git to skip the cache. GitHub maintains a standard one for Unity. Here are its most important lines:

Commit whenever something works: "Player jumps", "Saws hurt the player". If you'd rather not use Git yet, close Unity and zip the project folder without Library, Temp, and Logs. The zip stays small and opens on any computer with the same Editor version.

#Reading the Console

The Console's toolbar has three counters (messages, warnings, errors) that double as filters. Two toggles help too: Collapse merges identical lines, and Error Pause pauses the game the moment an error is logged. Double-clicking any error opens your code editor at the line that caused it.

Errors come in two kinds:

  • Compile errors (codes like CS0103) mean the code isn't valid C#. Nothing runs until they're fixed.
  • Runtime errors, or exceptions, happen while the game plays. The game keeps running, but the script that failed stops for that frame.

Here's a runtime error you'll meet often. This script is meant to change a sprite's color:

If you forget to drag a Sprite Renderer into the Target slot in the Inspector, pressing Play logs:

Read it bottom-up. The last line names the method, file, and line number (Tint.cs:9). The first line names the field that was empty. The fix is in the Inspector, not the code. Its cousin, NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object, means the same thing for a variable your code was supposed to fill, such as a GetComponent call that found nothing.

#A routine for getting unstuck

Fix the first error before any others. One missing semicolon can produce ten errors below it, and they all disappear together.

When you search or ask for help, give people what they need to answer: your Unity version (from the Hub), the exact error text, the script, and what you expected versus what happened. Good places to look are the Unity Manual and Scripting Reference (check the version picker says 6000.3) and the Unity Discussions forum.

#Comfort, privacy, and safety

  • Readable Editor. Preferences > General > Editor Theme switches between Light and Dark. The Editor follows your operating system's display scaling, so raise that if the text is small. Edit > Shortcuts (macOS: Unity > Shortcuts) lets you rebind any key.
  • Breaks. Game development is a lot of screen time. Every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
  • Privacy. Your Unity account holds your email and name; don't put either in a game you share. Keep real names, school names, and photos of people out of projects you post publicly.
  • Downloads. Asset packs and scripts run with your computer's permissions inside the Editor. Get them from the Unity Asset Store or creators you trust.
  • Players' safety. Flashing effects can trigger seizures. Keep any flashing effect to three flashes or fewer in any one second, and avoid large, bright red flashes.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Unity shows 14 errors after you edit one script. Where do you start?

  • Later errors are often side effects of the first one and vanish when it's fixed.

  • The last one is usually a consequence, not the cause.

  • Fixing an easy side effect wastes time if the real cause is still there.

Show answer

A. Later errors are often side effects of the first one and vanish when it's fixed.

2Which folder can you safely leave out of a backup?

  • That's your actual game.

  • It holds your layers, tags, physics, and input settings.

  • It's a cache that Unity rebuilds from Assets and Packages.

Show answer

C. It's a cache that Unity rebuilds from Assets and Packages.

3You move a sprite to a new folder using Finder, and objects now show "Missing". Why?

  • The file is fine; Unity just lost track of it.

  • Without the old .meta, Unity assigns a new ID and old references break. Move files inside the Project window.

  • They can, as long as you move them inside Unity.

Show answer

B. Without the old .meta, Unity assigns a new ID and old references break. Move files inside the Project window.

Key takeaways

  • Save scenes with Ctrl+S or ⌘S; Play mode changes are temporary unless you copy them out.
  • Back up Assets, Packages, and ProjectSettings; skip Library, Temp, and Logs.
  • Move and rename assets in the Project window so .meta files stay attached.
  • Fix the first Console error first, read stack traces for the file and line, and log values before guessing.

#Further reading

  • The Console window (opens in a new tab): every Console filter and option, including stack trace settings.
  • GitHub's Unity.gitignore (opens in a new tab): the full ignore file to copy into your project.
  • Unity Discussions (opens in a new tab): the official forum, where most error messages have already been asked about and answered.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe a GameObject as a container and explain what each common component adds.
  • Predict world positions from a parent's and child's Transform values.
  • Order the calls Unity makes to your scripts: Awake, OnEnable, Start, Update, LateUpdate.
  • Use prefabs, overrides, and variants so repeated objects stay consistent.

Picture a level with twelve spinning saw blades. You made one, then pressed Ctrl+D eleven times and dragged the copies into place. A playtester says the saws are too slow, so you click through all twelve and raise the speed. You miss one. Now a single saw in the middle of the level spins at half speed, and a month later someone files a bug about the "easy saw".

Copy-paste made twelve independent objects that happen to look alike. Unity's answer is the prefab, one saved definition all twelve follow. First, the model underneath it.

#A GameObject is an empty box; components are what it can do

Every object in a scene, whether a player, a saw, a camera, or an invisible spawn point, is a GameObject. On its own a GameObject does almost nothing. It has a name, a tag, a layer, and one Transform that says where it is.

Everything else comes from components you add to it. Select a saw in the Inspector and you might see:

Component What it adds
Transform Position, rotation, and scale (every GameObject has exactly one)
Sprite Renderer Draws an image, with a color tint and a sorting order
Circle Collider 2D A shape the physics engine can detect touching
Spinner (your script) Rotates the object every frame

For a saw that also bobs, you don't write a new kind of saw; you add a Bobber script to the same GameObject. Unity games are built from small one-job components combined on objects.

#Transforms, parents, and local positions

Drag one object onto another in the Hierarchy and it becomes a child. A child moves, rotates, and scales with its parent, and the numbers you see in its Inspector become local: measured from the parent, in the parent's scaled units.

Intuitively, a tooth sits "one unit right of the blade's center" wherever the blade goes, and if the blade doubles in size, so does that unit. Precisely: world position = parent position + the local position after the parent's scale and rotation are applied. Suppose:

  • Blade (parent): position (5, 2), scale (2, 2), rotation 0.
  • Tooth (child): local position (1, 0).

The tooth's world position is (5 + 2 × 1, 2 + 2 × 0) = (7, 2). Rotate the blade 90 degrees and the tooth swings around to (5, 4). This script prints both versions:

Attached to the tooth, it logs:

In code, transform.localPosition is what the Inspector shows for a child, and transform.position is always world space. Mixing them up is the most common reason an object teleports to the "wrong" place.

#Your scripts are components too

public class Spinner : MonoBehaviour defines a new kind of component, and each attached copy has its own fields. To reach another component on the same object, use GetComponent<T>():

GetComponent runs once in Awake and the result is kept in a field, rather than searched for every frame. [RequireComponent] adds a Sprite Renderer automatically if one is missing, so sprite can't be null. For objects elsewhere in the scene, use a [SerializeField] field and drag the object into its Inspector slot.

#When Unity calls your code: the frame loop

There's no main function in Unity. Unity calls specially named methods at set moments, in the same cycle every frame.

What each one is for:

  • Awake runs once, as soon as the object exists. Set up the object itself here, such as GetComponent calls.
  • Start runs once, just before the object's first Update. For objects in the scene when it loads, every Awake finishes before any Start begins, so in Start it's safe to talk to other objects.
  • Update runs every frame. Read input and move non-physics objects here.
  • FixedUpdate runs on a fixed clock (50 times a second by default), independent of frame rate. Physics code goes here, which Module 4 covers.
  • LateUpdate runs after every Update that frame, which makes it right for things that follow other things.

Suppose two objects in the scene, A and B, both have a script that logs each call. You'd see something like:

Whether A or B goes first isn't guaranteed, but both Awakes always come before either Start. Hence the rule: set yourself up in Awake, use others in Start.

#Prefabs: one definition, many copies

A prefab is a GameObject saved as an asset, with all its components, values, and children. Drag a configured saw from the Hierarchy into the Project window and it becomes Saw.prefab. Its name in the Hierarchy turns blue, which marks it as an instance of the prefab. Drag the prefab from the Project window into the scene as often as you like.

Three ideas make prefabs useful:

  1. Edit the prefab, every instance updates. Double-click the prefab asset to open Prefab Mode. Change the speed there, and all twelve saws change at once.
  2. Overrides. Change a value on one instance and that value is now overridden: its label turns bold with a blue bar beside it. The Overrides dropdown at the top of that instance's Inspector lets you Apply All (send the change to the prefab) or Revert All (go back to the prefab's value).
  3. Variants. Right-click a prefab and choose Create > Prefab Variant. The variant starts as an exact copy that keeps following its base, and you add or override only what's different, such as a bobbing saw that's also tinted orange. Change the base saw's sprite later and the variant gets it too.

Prefabs also work from code. Instantiate makes a new instance while the game runs:

Drag Saw.prefab from the Project window into Saw Prefab, press Play, and five saws appear two units apart, starting at the spawner. Quaternion.identity means "no rotation".

#Mistakes that cost an afternoon

⚠️ You changed an instance, and the others didn't follow

Editing a saw in the scene only changes that one saw; its fields go bold to show the override. If you meant to change all saws, use Overrides > Apply All on that instance, or make the change in Prefab Mode in the first place.

⚠️ NullReferenceException right after GetComponent

GetComponent<SpriteRenderer>() returns null when the component isn't on this GameObject. It's often on a child instead. Use GetComponentInChildren<SpriteRenderer>(), move the script to the object that has the component, or add [RequireComponent] so it can't be missing.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A parent is at position (3, 0) with scale (2, 2). Its child has local position (0, 1.5). Where is the child in the world?

  • That adds the local position without the parent's scale.

  • The local offset (0, 1.5) is scaled by 2 to (0, 3), then added to (3, 0).

  • That's the local position, which is relative to the parent, not the world.

Show answer

B. The local offset (0, 1.5) is scaled by 2 to (0, 3), then added to (3, 0).

2Script X uses another object's component in Awake, and that component is filled in by its own Awake. Sometimes X gets null. What's the fix?

  • It would work eventually, but it runs every frame and hides the real problem.

  • Every object's Awake finishes before any Start, so the other object is set up by then.

  • Script names don't control the call order.

Show answer

B. Every object's Awake finishes before any Start, so the other object is set up by then.

3You need ten saws that all spin, and two of them should also bob. What's the cleanest setup?

  • That's exactly the drift problem prefabs solve.

  • It works, but the bobbing saws are now one-off overrides that are easy to break.

  • Shared settings live in the base, and the variant adds only what's different.

Show answer

C. Shared settings live in the base, and the variant adds only what's different.

4Where should a camera that follows the player update its position?

  • Awake runs once; the camera must move every frame.

  • That's for physics and doesn't run in step with drawing.

  • It runs after every Update, so the player has already moved this frame.

Show answer

C. It runs after every Update, so the player has already moved this frame.

Key takeaways

  • A GameObject is a container. Its components (Transform, Sprite Renderer, colliders, your scripts) give it looks and behavior.
  • A child's Inspector values are local to its parent; transform.position is always the world position.
  • Unity calls Awake, then Start, then Update and LateUpdate every frame. Set yourself up in Awake and reach for other objects in Start.
  • Prefabs keep repeated objects in sync. Overrides customize one instance, and variants define a family of related objects.

#Further reading

  • GameObjects (opens in a new tab): the official explanation of GameObjects, components, tags, and layers.
  • Prefabs (opens in a new tab): Prefab Mode, overrides, nested prefabs, and variants in detail.
  • Order of execution for event functions (opens in a new tab): the complete diagram of every method Unity calls, and when.

What you'll learn

  • Build an object from a parent sprite, a child sprite, and a script component.
  • Turn it into a prefab, place instances, and edit them all at once in Prefab Mode.
  • Decide when to apply an override to the prefab and when to revert it.
  • Make a prefab variant that adds behavior while still following its base.

You're building the first stretch of the course's platformer level: a floor with four saw blades spinning on it and two more bobbing up and down in the air. The player arrives in Module 4. For now the goal is to set the level up so that every saw is controlled from one place.

Here is the structure you'll end up with:

And this is what the Hierarchy shows when you're done:

#Step 1: Folders and a floor

Open your UnityPlatformer project and the SampleScene scene (it's in Assets/Scenes). In the Project window, right-click Assets and create two folders, Scripts and Prefabs.

Now the floor:

  1. GameObject > 2D Object > Sprites > Square, and rename it Ground.
  2. In its Transform, set Position to (0, -3, 0) and Scale to (20, 1, 1).
  3. In the Sprite Renderer, set Color to a dark gray.
  4. Click Add Component, search for Box Collider 2D, and add it. Nothing uses it yet, but in Module 4 it's what the player stands on.

The square is 1 unit tall, so its top edge sits at y = -2.5. Press Ctrl+S (⌘S) to save the scene. Get in the habit now.

#Step 2: One saw, built by hand

  1. GameObject > 2D Object > Sprites > Circle. Rename it Saw, set Position to (-6, -2.2, 0), and make its color red.
  2. Right-click Saw in the Hierarchy and choose 2D Object > Sprites > Square. The new square is created as a child. Rename it Tooth.
  3. Give Tooth a Position of (0.5, 0, 0) and a Scale of (0.3, 0.3, 1), and color it near-black.
  4. In the Tooth's Sprite Renderer, set Order in Layer to 1 so it always draws on top of the red circle.

Why the tooth? A plain circle spinning looks exactly like a circle sitting still. The tooth, half a unit from the center in the parent's local space, swings around as the parent rotates, so you can see the spin. It's the parent-child Transform rule from the Notes doing real work.

#Step 3: Make it spin

In Assets/Scripts, create a MonoBehaviour script named Spinner and replace its contents:

Drag it onto Saw (the parent, not the tooth) and press Play. The tooth circles the blade clockwise, once every two seconds. In Unity's 2D view a positive Z rotation turns counterclockwise, so the negative default makes it turn clockwise. Stop Play mode before continuing.

#Step 4: Turn the saw into a prefab

Drag Saw from the Hierarchy into the Prefabs folder. Three things change:

  • A Saw asset with a blue cube icon appears in the Project window.
  • Saw in the Hierarchy turns blue. It's now an instance of that asset.
  • The top of its Inspector gains prefab controls, including the Overrides dropdown.

Now drag Saw.prefab from the Project window into the scene three more times. Unity names them Saw (1), Saw (2), and Saw (3). Set their positions to (-2, -2.2, 0), (2, -2.2, 0), and (6, -2.2, 0). Press Play: four saws spin in step.

#Step 5: Change every saw at once

Double-click Saw.prefab in the Project window. The Scene view switches to Prefab Mode and shows only the saw, and the Hierarchy shows the prefab's contents with a back arrow at the top.

In Prefab Mode, select the root Saw and change two things: set the Sprite Renderer color to orange, and set the Spinner's Degrees Per Second to -270. With Auto Save ticked in the Scene view's top bar, changes save as you make them; otherwise click Save.

Click the back arrow in the Hierarchy to return to the scene. All four saws are orange and spin faster. You changed one asset and the level followed. That's the whole problem from the start of the Notes, solved.

#Step 6: Override one saw, then decide what to do with it

Select Saw (3) in the scene and set its Degrees Per Second to -540. The field's label turns bold with a blue line in the margin: this instance now overrides the prefab's value.

Open the Overrides dropdown at the top of its Inspector. It lists exactly what differs from the prefab. You have two choices:

  • Revert All throws the override away and returns to -270.
  • Apply All pushes -540 into the prefab, which changes every saw.

Here you want one unusually fast saw near the end of the level, so keep the override and close the dropdown. A single override like this is fine. When you find yourself repeating the same overrides on several instances, that's the sign you need a variant.

#Step 7: A bobbing variant

Two saws should float and bob up and down. They're still saws (same look, same spin), with one extra behavior.

First, the behavior. Create a script named Bobber:

Mathf.Sin swings smoothly between -1 and 1, so the saw moves between 1.5 units below and 1.5 units above where it started. The position is always computed from startPosition, never from where the saw was last frame, so small timing differences can't add up into drift.

Now the variant:

  1. Right-click Saw.prefab in the Project window and choose Create > Prefab Variant. Name it BobbingSaw.
  2. Double-click BobbingSaw to open it in Prefab Mode, and add the Bobber component to its root.
  3. Return to the scene and drag BobbingSaw in twice. Place one at (-4, 0, 0) and the other at (4, 0, 0).
  4. On the second one, set Start Offset to 1, so the two move in opposite directions.

Press Play. Four saws spin on the floor, two more spin while floating up and down, and one floor saw spins noticeably faster.

#Step 8: Prove the family works

Open Saw.prefab (the base, not the variant) and change the Tooth's color to white. Return to the scene: every saw, including both bobbing ones, now has a white tooth. Variants inherit everything they don't override.

Then open BobbingSaw and change its color to purple. Only the two bobbing saws turn purple, because that's an override in the variant. The base saws stay orange. Save the scene and commit if you use Git: "Saw prefab and bobbing variant".

#The finished scripts

Both scripts are small on purpose. Each does one job, and the saw's behavior comes from which ones are attached.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the Saw need a Tooth child at all?

  • The tooth sits off-center in the parent's local space, so it orbits as the parent turns.

  • Spinner rotates whatever object it's on, child or not.

  • A prefab can be a single GameObject.

Show answer

A. The tooth sits off-center in the parent's local space, so it orbits as the parent turns.

2What would go wrong if Bobber did transform.position += new Vector3(0f, y, 0f) every frame?

  • It isn't: += adds this frame's offset on top of last frame's position.

  • Computing from the stored startPosition keeps the motion centered.

  • The code compiles fine; it just behaves badly.

Show answer

B. Computing from the stored startPosition keeps the motion centered.

3You want a red saw that spins backward, used in eight places. What's the best choice?

  • Eight copies of the same overrides will drift apart the first time you forget one.

  • The variant holds the differences once, and still inherits everything else from Saw.

  • That would make every saw red and backward, not just these eight.

Show answer

B. The variant holds the differences once, and still inherits everything else from Saw.

Key takeaways

  • Build an object once by hand, then drag it into the Project window to make it a prefab.
  • Edit the prefab in Prefab Mode to change every instance; bold fields on an instance are overrides.
  • One-off differences are fine as overrides. Repeated differences belong in a prefab variant.
  • Variants inherit every change to their base except the values they override.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Give each BobbingSaw a random Start Offset in Awake with Random.Range(0f, secondsPerCycle) so they never sync up.
  • Make a nested prefab: a floating platform (a Square with a Box Collider 2D) with two saws on top, saved as SawPlatform.prefab. Editing Saw.prefab still updates the saws inside it.
  • Add a Spinner to a Square to make a rotating bar hazard, and notice that you didn't write any new code.

#Further reading

  • Prefab Variants (opens in a new tab): how variants inherit, and how overrides stack when variants are nested.
  • Object.Instantiate (opens in a new tab): every way to spawn a prefab from code, including with a parent.

What you'll learn

  • Write small single-purpose components that change scale, color, and position over time.
  • Diagnose a NullReferenceException caused by GetComponent.
  • Predict when Awake and Start run for objects spawned during the game.
  • Spawn prefabs in grids, on timers, and in circles, with and without a parent.

Each exercise uses the UnityPlatformer project from the build-along. Make a new scene for practice so your level stays clean: in the Project window, select SampleScene, press Ctrl+D (⌘D) to duplicate it, rename the copy Practice, open it, and delete everything except Main Camera and Global Light 2D.

#Warm-up

A parent sits at (2, 1) with rotation 180 degrees and scale (1, 1). Its child has local position (1, 0). Where is the child in world space?

Rotating 180 degrees turns the offset (1, 0) into (-1, 0), and adding the parent's position gives (1, 1). If you got (3, 1), you added the local offset without rotating it first.

#Exercise 1: A pulsing coin

Make a yellow Circle named Coin and write a Pulser component that makes it grow and shrink between its original size and 1.2 times that size, once per second. The inspector should expose the amount and the speed.

Sample result: the coin smoothly breathes in and out, and if you set its scale to (0.5, 0.5, 1) before pressing Play, it pulses between 0.5 and 0.6, not between 1 and 1.2.

Need a hint?

Store transform.localScale once, before anything changes it. Then copy the idea behind Bobber: compute a value between 0 and 1 from Time.time each frame and set the scale from the stored original, never from last frame's scale.

Show solution

Saving baseScale in Awake is what makes a half-size coin pulse around half size. Multiplying a Vector3 by a float scales all three axes at once.

#Exercise 2: Why is the tint script crashing?

A teammate wrote this to color the saw's tooth when the game starts, and attached it to the root Saw object:

It works on most saws but one throws:

Explain the cause and make the script safe, using a reference set in the Inspector instead of searching by name.

Need a hint?

transform.Find searches children by exact name. What happens if someone renamed the child on one instance to Tooth (1) or deleted it? And what does Find return then?

Show solution

transform.Find("Tooth") returns null when no child has that exact name, and line 10 then calls GetComponent on null. Renaming a child breaks name searches silently. A serialized reference doesn't care about names:

Open Saw.prefab and drag its Tooth child into the Tooth slot once; every instance gets the reference. Passing this as the second argument to Debug.LogWarning makes the Console highlight the broken object when you click the message.

#Exercise 3: Predict the order for spawned objects

Spawner makes a coin when you press C. Both scripts log their calls:

The coin prefab has a LoggingCoin script that logs Awake, OnEnable, and Start. Write down the five lines in the order you expect after one press, then test.

Need a hint?

Instantiate doesn't return until the new object exists and is set up. Which of the three calls counts as "setting up", and which one waits until just before the coin's first Update?

Show solution

Awake and OnEnable run inside Instantiate, before it returns. Start is deferred until just before the coin's first Update. This is why it's safe to configure a spawned object right after Instantiate returns (for example, setting its speed) and have its Start see the new value.

#Exercise 4: A grid of coins

Write CoinGrid, which spawns a grid of coin prefabs in Start: 5 columns and 3 rows, 1.5 units apart, with the first coin at the spawner's position. Every coin should be a child of the spawner, so moving the spawner moves the whole grid.

Sample Hierarchy after pressing Play:

Need a hint?

Use one loop inside another, one for rows and one for columns. Instantiate has an overload with a fourth argument, the parent Transform.

Show solution

With the parent argument, each clone appears under CoinGrid in the Hierarchy. The position argument is still in world space, which is why it adds transform.position.

#Exercise 5: Falling rocks on a timer

Make a Rock prefab (a gray Square) with a Faller script that moves it down at a set speed and destroys it after 4 seconds. Then write RockSpawner, which spawns a rock every 1.5 seconds at a random x between -7 and 7, at the spawner's height.

Sample result: rocks rain down at a steady rhythm, and the Hierarchy never holds more than three or so at a time.

Need a hint?

For the timer, keep a float that counts down by Time.deltaTime each frame; when it reaches zero, spawn and reset it. Destroy(gameObject, 4f) schedules a destroy for later, so it can go in Start. Random.Range(-7f, 7f) gives a random float.

Show solution

Each rock lives 4 seconds and a new one arrives every 1.5, so about three exist at once. timer starts at 0, which spawns the first rock immediately.

#Exercise 6: Plan a coin family

Your level needs silver coins worth 1 point and gold coins worth 5. Gold coins are yellow, 1.3 times bigger, and pulse; silver coins are gray and still. Both spin slowly, and both should change together if you later swap the art.

Decide which prefab is the base, which is the variant, and which values live where. Then build it, using a CoinValue script with a serialized int points.

Need a hint?

Put everything the two coins share in the base. The variant should hold only differences. Is the Pulser a difference or a shared trait?

Show solution

Make Coin.prefab the base: Circle sprite, Spinner (slow, about -60), CoinValue with Points 1, gray color. That base is the silver coin.

Make GoldCoin a variant of it, with these overrides: Points 5, yellow color, scale (1.3, 1.3, 1), plus an added Pulser component. Because Pulser exists only in the variant, it's a difference, not a shared trait.

Swap the base coin's sprite later and gold coins pick it up too, while keeping their own color, size, and value. Points is a read-only property, so other scripts can read a coin's value without being able to change it.

#Challenge: A ring of orbiting saws

Write SawRing, which spawns count saws evenly spaced on a circle of a given radius around the spawner, as its children. Then add a Spinner to the spawner itself. The whole ring should rotate while each saw keeps spinning on its own.

Here's where the six saws land for count = 6 and radius = 2. Each saw sits at an angle of i × 360° / count from the right-hand side:

Need a hint?

Unity's Mathf.Cos and Mathf.Sin take radians, so convert with Mathf.PI (or multiply degrees by Mathf.Deg2Rad). Spawn each saw at transform.position plus the offset, and pass transform as the parent so the ring's rotation carries the saws around.

Show solution

Give the SawRing object a Spinner with a slow speed such as 45. Two rotations now stack: the ring's Spinner turns the parent, which carries every child around the circle, and each saw's own Spinner turns it in place. Neither script knows about the other.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why movement must be scaled by Time.deltaTime, and predict what happens without it.
  • Avoid the C# mistakes that come up in Unity scripts: float literals, integer division, and mixing Vector2 with Vector3.
  • Expose tunable values with [SerializeField], and know why the Inspector value wins over the code.
  • Read keys with Keyboard.current, build a movement vector, and normalize it.
  • Flip a character to face its direction of travel.

You test your game at home and the hero crosses the screen in four seconds. Your friend's gaming laptop runs it at 144 frames per second, and the hero crosses in under two. Same code, same level. The script says transform.position += Vector3.right * 0.1f; inside Update, which means "0.1 units per frame". More frames per second means more distance per second.

This module's job is movement that feels identical everywhere. It comes down to one idea and a handful of C# details.

#Movement is a rate, not a step

Think of a car's speedometer. "60 miles per hour" says how far you go per unit of time, and the distance after a trip is speed times time. Frames are just how often you check in.

In Unity, Time.deltaTime is the number of seconds since the previous frame: about 0.0167 at 60 FPS and about 0.0069 at 144 FPS. Multiply a speed in units per second by it and you get the distance for this frame:

At 60 FPS each frame moves less than it would at 30 FPS, but there are twice as many frames, so a second of play covers exactly speed units either way. Step through this model of both versions, written in Python so you can watch every frame. It moves "0.5 per frame" on one line and "speed × deltaTime" on the next, at 4 and 8 frames per second:

The per-frame version doubles its distance when the frame rate doubles. The deltaTime version lands on 5.0 both times. Real frame rates also wobble from frame to frame, which the per-frame version turns into visible stutter.

#C# details that trip people up in Unity

Unity's math uses float, not double, and C# is strict about that.

  • Float literals need an f. float speed = 5.5; fails with error CS0664: Literal of type double cannot be implicitly converted to type 'float'; use an 'F' suffix to create a literal of this type. Write 5.5f. Whole numbers like 5 are fine without it.
  • Integer division drops the fraction. float half = 1 / 2; stores 0, because both sides are integers, so the division happens before the conversion. Write 1f / 2f.
  • Vector2 and Vector3 don't mix in arithmetic. Each converts to the other automatically, so transform.position + someVector2 is ambiguous and fails with error CS0034: Operator '+' is ambiguous on operands of type 'Vector3' and 'Vector2'. Cast one side explicitly: transform.position + (Vector3)move.
  • Fields remember; locals forget. A variable declared inside Update is created fresh every frame. Anything that must last between frames, like the current velocity or a cooldown timer, belongs in a field on the class.

#Tune it in the Inspector

Hard-coding speed = 5f means editing code and waiting for a recompile every time you want to try 6. Serialized fields put the value in the Inspector instead:

[SerializeField] shows a private field in the Inspector and saves its value with the scene or prefab, while other scripts still can't change it. That's usually better than public, which also shows in the Inspector but lets any script anywhere write to it. [Range] turns the field into a slider, [Header] adds a bold label above it, and [Tooltip] shows a hint on hover.

⚠️ You changed the default in code and nothing happened

Once a component exists, the Inspector stores its own copy of every serialized value. Changing speed = 5f to speed = 8f in the script affects only components added after the change. Existing ones keep 5. Change the value in the Inspector, or open the component's menu and choose Reset to reload the code defaults.

#Direction times speed, and why diagonals need fixing

A Vector2 is an arrow: an x part and a y part. For movement it helps to split it into a direction (which way) and a speed (how fast). Pressing right gives the direction (1, 0). Pressing up gives (0, 1). Pressing both gives (1, 1), which is longer:

A length of 1.414 means a player holding two keys moves 41% faster than one holding a single key. Normalizing divides a vector by its own length, keeping the direction and setting the length to 1. In Unity that's input.normalized. Multiply the normalized direction by your speed and every direction moves at the same rate.

#Reading the keyboard with the Input System

This course reads devices directly. Keyboard.current is the keyboard in use (or null if there isn't one), and each key is a control with three questions you can ask:

Property True when Use it for
isPressed Every frame the key is held Walking, sprinting
wasPressedThisFrame Only the frame it goes down Jumping, dashing, menu selection
wasReleasedThisFrame Only the frame it comes up Cutting a jump short, releasing a charge

Building a movement direction from WASD and the arrow keys looks like this:

Holding A and D together gives x = 0, so opposite keys cancel instead of one winning. The null check matters on machines without a keyboard; without it, the first line that touches keyboard.aKey would throw a NullReferenceException.

⚠️ InvalidOperationException: You are trying to read Input using the UnityEngine.Input class

Many older tutorials use Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") or Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space). That's the old Input Manager. When Active Input Handling is set to Input System Package (New), every one of those calls throws this exception. Translate them instead: Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space) becomes Keyboard.current.spaceKey.isPressed, and Input.GetKeyDown becomes wasPressedThisFrame.

#Facing the way you move

Most 2D characters are drawn facing right. To face left, mirror them. There are two ways, and they behave differently:

  • SpriteRenderer.flipX = true mirrors only that one sprite. Children (a sword, a hat, an eye) and colliders don't flip.
  • Setting transform.localScale.x to a negative value mirrors the object and everything under it.

Use flipX for a single sprite and the scale method when children must follow. Either way, only change facing when there's horizontal input. If you set facing from input.x every frame, releasing the keys gives 0 and the character snaps back to facing right.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A script does transform.position += Vector3.right * 0.1f; in Update. The game runs at 30 FPS on one laptop and 120 FPS on another. How far does the object move in one second on each?

  • That's the distance per frame, not per second.

  • It moves 0.1 every frame, so distance per second is 0.1 times the frame rate.

  • It would only be the same on both if the step were multiplied by Time.deltaTime.

Show answer

B. It moves 0.1 every frame, so distance per second is 0.1 times the frame rate.

2A player holds W and D with this code: transform.position += (Vector3)(input * speed * Time.deltaTime);, and speed is 4. How fast do they move?

  • That's true only if input is normalized first.

  • input is (1, 1), whose length is 1.414, and 1.414 × 4 ≈ 5.66.

  • The x and y parts aren't added; the speed is the length of the combined vector.

Show answer

B. input is (1, 1), whose length is 1.414, and 1.414 × 4 ≈ 5.66.

3Which key property should trigger a jump?

  • It's true every frame the key is held, so holding Space would try to jump every frame.

  • It's true only on the frame the key goes down, so one press means one jump.

  • That fires when the key comes up, which would delay every jump.

Show answer

B. It's true only on the frame the key goes down, so one press means one jump.

4Your character has a child torch. When it faces left with spriteRenderer.flipX = true, the torch stays on the right side. Why?

  • Use a negative localScale.x on the parent so children mirror too.

  • They can, by flipping the parent's scale.

  • That would mirror the torch image in place, but it would still sit on the right.

Show answer

A. Use a negative localScale.x on the parent so children mirror too.

Key takeaways

  • Write speeds in units per second and multiply by Time.deltaTime every frame.
  • Use f on decimal literals, avoid integer division, and cast when mixing Vector2 and Vector3.
  • Prefer [SerializeField] private fields for tuning; the Inspector's saved value overrides the code default.
  • Build input from Keyboard.current, normalize it so diagonals aren't faster, and only update facing when x isn't zero.

#Further reading

  • Time.deltaTime (opens in a new tab): the official reference, including what deltaTime returns inside FixedUpdate.
  • SerializeField (opens in a new tab): which field types Unity can save, and the rules for serialization.
  • Input System: Keyboard support (opens in a new tab): every key control and how keyboard layouts affect key names.

What you'll learn

  • Turn keyboard input into frame-rate-independent movement, and measure the result.
  • Fix fast diagonals with normalization, and add acceleration with Vector2.MoveTowards.
  • Add a sprint key, flip the character with its children, and keep it inside an arena.
  • Organize a growing script into small methods with Inspector-tunable fields.

You're building the control script for a top-down explorer, the kind of view used in Zelda-style adventures and farming games. When it's finished, the explorer:

  • walks with WASD or the arrow keys at the same speed in all eight directions,
  • speeds up and slows down smoothly instead of starting and stopping instantly,
  • sprints while Left Shift is held,
  • turns to face left or right, eye included,
  • can't leave the arena.

Its Inspector will look like this:

Physics and collisions come in Module 4. This explorer moves its Transform directly, which is the right tool for learning how movement math works.

#Step 1: A scene for the explorer

In the Project window, select SampleScene and press Ctrl+D (⌘D) to duplicate it. Rename the copy TopDown and double-click to open it. Delete the ground and all the saws, keeping Main Camera and Global Light 2D.

Add a floor to walk on: GameObject > 2D Object > Sprites > Square, named Arena, at position (0, 0, 0), scale (16, 9, 1), dark green, with its Sprite Renderer's Order in Layer set to -1 so it draws behind everything. The camera's default view is 10 units tall, so the whole arena fits on screen.

#Step 2: The explorer and its eye

  1. GameObject > 2D Object > Sprites > Capsule. Name it Explorer, set scale to (0.8, 0.8, 1), and color it blue. The Capsule shape is 1 by 2 units, so the explorer ends up 0.8 wide and 1.6 tall.
  2. Right-click Explorer and add a child 2D Object > Sprites > Square named Eye. Set its position to (0.25, 0.5, 0), scale to (0.25, 0.25, 1), color to white, and Order in Layer to 1.

The eye sits on the right side of the head, so you'll always see which way the explorer faces.

#Step 3: First movement, with a speedometer

In Assets/Scripts, create a MonoBehaviour script named TopDownMover and attach it to Explorer. Start with the simplest version that works, plus a temporary log that prints the speed:

Press Play, click in the Game view, and hold D, then W and D together. With Collapse on in the Console, you'll see:

Dividing the step by Time.deltaTime turns "distance this frame" back into "distance per second", so the log reads 4.00 whatever your frame rate is. The second line is the diagonal bug from the Notes, measured.

#Step 4: Same speed in every direction

Add one line right after reading the input:

sqrMagnitude is the length squared. Comparing it with 1 asks "is this longer than 1?" without computing a square root, and the check leaves (0, 0) alone. Press Play and hold W and D: the log now reads 4.00. Delete the Debug.Log lines once you've seen it.

#Step 5: Smooth starts and stops

Right now the explorer jumps from 0 to full speed in one frame. Real movement has a little acceleration. The fix is to keep a velocity that lasts between frames and nudge it toward the speed you want:

Vector2.MoveTowards(current, target, maxDelta) moves current toward target by at most maxDelta, without overshooting. With acceleration 30, the explorer reaches 4 units/s in about 0.13 seconds.

Time.deltaTime now appears twice, and both are needed. The first scales how much the velocity may change this frame (units per second, per second). The second scales how far the position moves at that velocity. Set Acceleration to 4 in the Inspector while playing and the explorer slides around as if on ice; 60 feels almost instant.

#Step 6: Sprint

Add a field and pick the speed before computing the target:

Because the sprint changes only the target, the acceleration from Step 5 still applies: pressing Shift ramps up to 7 units/s rather than snapping there.

#Step 7: Face the way you're going

flipX would mirror the capsule but leave the eye behind, so flip with the scale instead:

Call FaceDirection(input.x); at the end of Update. Mathf.Abs keeps the size you set (0.8), and Mathf.Sign supplies the direction, so the explorer flips without growing or shrinking. Facing follows the input, not the velocity, so the explorer turns the instant you press the other key, while its body is still decelerating.

#Step 8: Arena walls

The explorer can walk off the green floor. Clamp the next position to a rectangle centered on the origin:

Why 15.2 by 7.4 and not 16 by 9? The clamp limits the explorer's center. Shrinking the area by the explorer's own width (0.8) and height (1.6) keeps its whole body on the floor.

Zeroing the velocity when you hit a wall matters more than it looks. Without it, pushing into a wall keeps the velocity at full speed, and when you reverse, the explorer spends a moment decelerating from a speed it wasn't really moving at. The walls feel sticky.

To see the limits while editing, add this method; it draws a yellow outline whenever Explorer is selected:

#The finished script

Press Play for a final test: all eight directions feel equally fast, Shift sprints, releasing the keys glides to a stop, the eye flips with the body, and every wall stops you cleanly.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does facing use input.x instead of velocity.x?

  • Velocity lags behind input because of acceleration; facing based on it would feel delayed.

  • Velocity is negative when moving left.

  • Mathf.Sign works on any float.

Show answer

A. Velocity lags behind input because of acceleration; facing based on it would feel delayed.

2In Step 8, what happens if you remove the two lines that zero the velocity at a wall?

  • The clamp still holds the position inside the arena.

  • The stored velocity stays at full speed into the wall, so turning around starts by decelerating from it.

  • Nothing about the code becomes invalid.

Show answer

B. The stored velocity stays at full speed into the wall, so turning around starts by decelerating from it.

3Why is the arena size 15.2 × 7.4 when the floor is 16 × 9?

  • It's about the explorer's size, not decoration.

  • Half of 0.8 on each side and half of 1.6 on top and bottom keeps the whole body on the floor.

  • The whole 16 × 9 floor is on screen.

Show answer

B. Half of 0.8 on each side and half of 1.6 on top and bottom keeps the whole body on the floor.

Key takeaways

  • Measure movement with a log of distance / Time.deltaTime to prove it's frame-rate independent.
  • Normalize input only when it's longer than 1, and keep velocity in a field so acceleration can shape it.
  • Change the target speed for sprinting; let acceleration handle the transition.
  • Flip with localScale when children must follow, and zero velocity at walls so they don't feel sticky.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add separate acceleration and deceleration values, so the explorer starts quickly but glides to a stop.
  • Replace the fixed arena with one read from the Arena sprite's bounds: GetComponent<SpriteRenderer>().bounds on a serialized reference.
  • Read the gamepad too: Gamepad.current?.leftStick.ReadValue() returns a Vector2 you can add to the keyboard input before normalizing.

#Further reading

  • Vector2.MoveTowards (opens in a new tab): the exact behavior of maxDistanceDelta, including negative values.
  • Gizmos (opens in a new tab): every shape you can draw in the Scene view to visualize ranges, paths, and limits.

What you'll learn

  • Read and fix the compile errors that movement code produces most often.
  • Test frame-rate independence by changing the frame rate on purpose.
  • Use countdown timers for a dash and its cooldown.
  • Convert the mouse position from screen pixels to world units.
  • Move in discrete steps, wrap around the screen with LateUpdate, and aim with Mathf.Atan2.

Work in the TopDown scene from the build-along unless an exercise says otherwise. Keep your finished TopDownMover safe; when an exercise changes it, make a copy first (Ctrl+D or ⌘D on the script) and rename both the file and the class.

#Warm-up

speed is 3 and the game runs at a steady 50 FPS, so Time.deltaTime is 0.02. How far does speed * Time.deltaTime move the player each frame, and after one second?

Each frame moves 3 × 0.02 = 0.06 units. Fifty frames make one second, and 50 × 0.06 = 3 units, which is exactly speed. That's the point of multiplying by deltaTime.

#Exercise 1: Three compile errors

This script won't compile. Fix all three errors without changing what it's meant to do (move right at 2.5 units per second, starting half a unit up).

The Console shows:

Need a hint?

Only two errors are reported, but there are three bugs. One of them compiles fine and quietly produces the wrong number. Which expression in Start involves two integers?

Show solution

2.5 is a double, so it needs the f. 1 / 2 is integer division, which gives 0 with no error, so the object started at y = 0 instead of 0.5. The cast tells C# which of the two automatic conversions you mean.

#Exercise 2: Prove it with the frame rate

Write a FrameRateSwitcher component that sets the game to 15 FPS when you press 1, 60 FPS on 2, and 240 FPS on 3, and logs the change. Put it on the Main Camera, then hold D and watch the explorer at each setting.

Sample output:

At 15 FPS the movement looks choppy but covers the same distance per second as at 240.

Need a hint?

Application.targetFrameRate is ignored while V-Sync is on, so set QualitySettings.vSyncCount = 0 first. The number keys above the letters are digit1Key, digit2Key, and digit3Key.

Show solution

In the Editor, the target affects the Game view, which is where Play mode runs. Try deleting * Time.deltaTime from a copy of the mover and switching rates: the explorer becomes 16 times faster at 240 than at 15.

#Exercise 3: A dash with a cooldown

Add a dash to a copy of TopDownMover. Pressing Space launches the explorer in its current input direction at 16 units per second for 0.15 seconds. After a dash, Space does nothing for 0.8 seconds. With no keys held, the dash goes the way the explorer faces.

Need a hint?

Keep two countdown floats, dashTimeLeft and cooldownLeft, and subtract Time.deltaTime from both every frame. While dashTimeLeft > 0, set the velocity straight to the dash velocity instead of using MoveTowards. The facing direction is the sign of transform.localScale.x.

Show solution

Add these fields:

Then replace the velocity part of Update with:

input is already normalized, so diagonal dashes aren't longer. When the dash ends, MoveTowards takes over from dash speed, which gives a short slide out of it. The cooldown starts at the dash's own length plus 0.8, so the 0.8 seconds count from when the dash finishes.

#Exercise 4: Follow the mouse

Make a small Circle named Firefly with a MouseFollower script that flies toward the mouse pointer at 5 units per second and stops on it, without overshooting.

Need a hint?

Mouse.current.position.ReadValue() is in screen pixels. Camera.main.ScreenToWorldPoint converts it, but for an orthographic camera the result's z is the camera's z (-10). An object at the camera's depth is invisible, so set z to 0.

Show solution

Without target.z = 0f, the firefly "disappears" the moment you press Play: it moves to z = -10, the camera's own position, which is closer than the camera's near clipping plane. MoveTowards never overshoots, so the firefly settles exactly on the pointer.

#Exercise 5: Wrap around the screen

Write a ScreenWrap component: when the object leaves one edge of the camera's view, it reappears at the opposite edge, like the ship in Asteroids. It should work alongside any movement script. Test it on the explorer with Arena Size set to (100, 100) so the clamp doesn't interfere.

Need a hint?

The camera's half-height in world units is orthographicSize, and the half-width is that times aspect. Do the wrap in LateUpdate, which runs after every Update, so the mover has already moved this frame.

Show solution

Measuring from the camera's position means the wrap still works if the camera moves. Because it's a separate component, the same script can wrap asteroids, bullets, or the player.

#Exercise 6: Tile-by-tile movement

Write a GridMover for a puzzle-style game: holding an arrow key moves the object exactly one unit in that direction, sliding smoothly over 1/6 of a second, and it can't change direction halfway through a tile. It should start snapped to the nearest whole-number position.

Need a hint?

Store a target position and a moving flag. While moving, MoveTowards the target and ignore input; when you arrive, clear the flag. Read input only when not moving. Mathf.Round snaps a float to the nearest whole number.

Show solution

Using isPressed lets a held key walk tile after tile; wasPressedThisFrame would require one tap per tile, which suits some puzzle games better. Returning early from ReadStep means only one direction counts, so there are no diagonal steps.

#Challenge: A turret that aims and fires

Build a stationary turret in the middle of the arena: a Square Turret with a child Barrel (a thin rectangle sticking out to the right). The barrel rotates to point at the mouse at all times, and a left click fires a bullet prefab from the barrel in the direction it's pointing. Bullets fly at 12 units per second and disappear after 2 seconds.

Mathf.Atan2(y, x) turns a direction into an angle, measured counterclockwise from the right. Note the argument order: y comes first.

Need a hint?

Get the mouse's world position as in Exercise 4, subtract the barrel's position to get a direction, convert it with Atan2 and Mathf.Rad2Deg, and set the barrel's rotation with Quaternion.Euler(0f, 0f, angle). A bullet can move along its own transform.right, so spawning it with the barrel's rotation is all the aiming it needs.

Show solution

For the barrel to pivot around the turret instead of its own middle, make Barrel an empty child at the turret's center, and put the thin rectangle sprite inside it, offset to the right. Rotating the empty swings the sprite around the center, the same parent-child trick as the saw's tooth in Module 2. Point the turret's Barrel slot at the empty.
