m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Choose between Dynamic, Kinematic, and Static bodies, and move a Rigidbody 2D the right way.
  • Explain the fixed physics clock, and split work between Update and FixedUpdate.
  • Predict when OnCollisionEnter2D and OnTriggerEnter2D fire, and use the data they pass.
  • Prevent tunneling with Continuous collision detection.
  • Filter physics with layers, and set up a follow camera that doesn't make players queasy.

Put a wall in the top-down scene from Module 3 and walk at it. The explorer slides straight through. Nothing is broken: the script sets transform.position, and a Transform is just three numbers. Nothing in that code ever asks "is something in the way?"

A platformer asks it constantly: fall, land, stop at walls, notice coins and saws. Unity's 2D physics engine answers it once you hand movement over to it.

#Who moves the object: the Transform or the Rigidbody

Add a Rigidbody 2D and the physics engine owns the object's position: each step it applies gravity and velocity, checks overlaps, and pushes things apart. The Body Type sets how much control physics has:

Body Type Moved by Pushed by others? Use it for
Dynamic Gravity, forces, and velocity you set Yes The player, crates, falling rocks
Kinematic Only your script (linearVelocity or MovePosition) No Moving platforms, scripted enemies
Static Nothing; it doesn't move No Walls and ground

An object with a collider and no Rigidbody 2D at all behaves like Static, which is how most level geometry works.

The rule that follows: once an object has a Rigidbody 2D, move it through the Rigidbody with rb.linearVelocity, rb.AddForce, or rb.MovePosition. Writing transform.position every frame teleports it behind the engine's back, causing jitter and sinking. (Older tutorials call linearVelocity by its pre-Unity 6 name, velocity.)

#Colliders give the engine a shape

A Rigidbody 2D says how something moves; a collider says what shape it is: Box, Circle, Capsule, or Polygon Collider 2D, sized to the sprite automatically. Objects interact only through colliders, so a Rigidbody 2D with no collider falls through everything.

Friction comes from a Physics Material 2D (Assets > Create > 2D > Physics Material 2D) in a collider's Material slot. A player with normal friction who holds right against a wall sticks to it in mid-air, because wall friction cancels gravity. Friction 0 on the player fixes it.

#Physics runs on its own clock

Frames come 30, 60, or 144 times a second, but physics steps every 0.02 seconds (Edit > Project Settings > Time > Fixed Timestep). Unity banks elapsed time and runs as many steps as fit, calling FixedUpdate before each. This model shows the result frame by frame:

At 144 FPS most frames run no physics step at all. At 30 FPS some frames run two. That's the reason for the usual split:

  • Read input in Update. wasPressedThisFrame is true for exactly one frame. If you check it in FixedUpdate, a frame with zero steps misses the press entirely, and a frame with two steps sees it twice.
  • Change velocity and apply forces in FixedUpdate. That keeps physics changes in step with the physics engine.

Stepping slower than the screen makes a body appear to move in small jumps. Setting the Rigidbody 2D's Interpolate to Interpolate draws it between physics positions, which removes the stutter.

#Tunneling: when fast objects skip walls

By default each step checks overlaps only at the new positions (Discrete detection), so something fast can be before a thin wall at one step and past it at the next:

At 60 units per second the bullet moves 1.2 units per step and hops a 0.5-unit wall. Setting the Rigidbody 2D's Collision Detection to Continuous sweeps the shape along its path between steps. It costs more, so save it for small, fast bodies like the player and bullets.

#Collisions versus triggers

Every collider has an Is Trigger checkbox:

  • Off (solid): objects can't overlap, and when two touch, both get OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision). For ground, walls, and bouncing things.
  • On (trigger): objects pass through, and both get OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other). For coins, hazards, checkpoints, and zones.

In both cases, at least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody 2D, or no event is sent. For two solid colliders, make that a Dynamic one: by default a Kinematic body doesn't generate collisions with Static colliders. There are matching Stay and Exit methods (OnTriggerExit2D, for example) for "still touching" and "stopped touching."

A trigger event passes only the other collider, since nothing physical happened. A collision passes a Collision2D with details like relativeVelocity, how fast the two met, which a crate could use for a louder thud on harder landings. CompareTag("Player") checks the Tag set at the top of the Inspector.

#Layers decide who interacts with whom

Every GameObject has one Layer (the dropdown at the top right of the Inspector; Add Layer... makes new ones). Layers do two physics jobs:

  • The Layer Collision Matrix (Edit > Project Settings > Physics 2D, Layer Collision Matrix tab) says which layers can touch at all. Untick Enemy against Enemy and enemies pass through each other but still stand on the ground.
  • Physics queries take a LayerMask, a set of layers to look for. The build-along uses one to ask "is there ground under my feet?" without counting the player's own collider.

#Cameras that follow without making people sick

A 2D camera is orthographic, and its Size is half the view's height in world units. How a follow camera moves decides how the game feels, and for some players whether they feel sick. The trouble is motion the player didn't cause or can't predict: rigid locking to a jittery body, snapping on every turn, constant shake. Good follow cameras use three ideas:

  • Damping: the camera eases toward the player instead of matching it every frame.
  • A dead zone: a box mid-screen where the player can move without the camera moving, absorbing small back-and-forth steps.
  • Bounds: the camera stops at the level's edges instead of showing empty space.

Cinemachine, a free Unity package, provides all three: a Cinemachine Camera with a Position Composer frames a Tracking Target, a Cinemachine Brain on the Main Camera applies the result, and a Cinemachine Confiner 2D extension adds bounds.

#The mistake that makes events silently fail

⚠️ OnCollisionEnter (3D) in a 2D game

void OnCollisionEnter(Collision c) and void OnTriggerEnter(Collider c) are the 3D versions. In a 2D game they compile and never run. Use the 2D names. If you write the 2D name with a 3D parameter type, Unity logs Script error: OnCollisionEnter2D followed by "This message parameter has to be of type: Collision2D" and "The message will be ignored."

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A coin has a Circle Collider 2D with Is Trigger on, and no Rigidbody 2D. The player has a Dynamic Rigidbody 2D and a Capsule Collider 2D. What happens when they overlap?

  • One Rigidbody 2D in the pair is enough, and a trigger never blocks movement.

  • Only one of the two needs a Rigidbody 2D.

  • A trigger collider produces trigger events, not collisions.

Show answer

A. One Rigidbody 2D in the pair is enough, and a trigger never blocks movement.

2A jump script checks Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame inside FixedUpdate. At 144 FPS, what will players notice?

  • That's the risk at low frame rates, when one frame can run two physics steps.

  • Most frames at 144 FPS run no FixedUpdate, so the one frame where the press is true is often skipped.

  • FixedUpdate doesn't run every frame, so it can miss one-frame events.

Show answer

B. Most frames at 144 FPS run no FixedUpdate, so the one frame where the press is true is often skipped.

3Players say the camera "lurches" every time they tap left and right. What's the gentlest fix?

  • Rigid locking passes every small movement straight to the screen.

  • Small movements inside the dead zone don't move the camera, and damping eases the rest.

  • Shake adds more unplanned motion, the main cause of discomfort.

Show answer

B. Small movements inside the dead zone don't move the camera, and damping eases the rest.

Key takeaways

  • Dynamic bodies for the player, Kinematic for scripted movers, Static or none for level geometry; move bodies with linearVelocity, not the Transform.
  • Read input in Update, change velocity in FixedUpdate, and interpolate the player.
  • Solids send OnCollisionEnter2D, triggers send OnTriggerEnter2D, and one of the pair needs a Rigidbody 2D.
  • Continuous detection stops tunneling, layers filter contacts, and damping, a dead zone, and bounds make a comfortable camera.

#Further reading

  • Introduction to Rigidbody 2D (opens in a new tab): Unity's explanation of body types and why colliders should be moved through the Rigidbody.
  • MonoBehaviour.OnTriggerEnter2D (opens in a new tab): the trigger event's exact rules and an example.
  • Cinemachine Position Composer (opens in a new tab): every framing setting for 2D follow cameras, including dead zones and lookahead.

What you'll learn

  • Set up a Dynamic Rigidbody 2D player with a capsule collider, no friction, Continuous detection, and interpolation.
  • Read input in Update, apply velocity in FixedUpdate, and jump only when a layer-filtered ground check passes.
  • Make every saw a hazard by editing one prefab, and add trigger coins.
  • Install Cinemachine and build a follow camera with damping, a dead zone, and level bounds.

The hazard course from Module 2 becomes a game. A/D or the arrows run, Space jumps (only from the ground), any saw sends you back to the start, coins vanish when grabbed, and the camera glides after you without showing empty space past the level's edges.

#Step 1: Widen the level and give it a Ground layer

Open SampleScene. A follow camera only matters in a level wider than the screen, so set Ground to position (10, -3, 0) and scale (40, 1, 1); it now runs from x = -10 to x = 30.

Add four more Squares, each with a Box Collider 2D:

Name Position Scale Purpose
Platform A (11, -0.5, 0) (4, 0.5, 1) First jump
Platform B (17, 1.5, 0) (4, 0.5, 1) Second jump
Wall (24, -1, 0) (1, 3, 1) A wall to jump against
Left Wall (-10.5, 2, 0) (1, 10, 1) Stops you walking off the left end

Now the layer. Open the Layer dropdown at the top right of the Inspector, choose Add Layer..., and type Ground into the first empty User Layer slot. Then select Ground and the four new objects together and set their Layer to Ground. Leave the saws on Default.

  1. GameObject > 2D Object > Sprites > Capsule, named Player, at (-8, -1.5, 0), scale (0.8, 0.8, 1), blue, with the same Eye child as in Module 3.
  2. Set its Tag to Player, one of Unity's built-in tags.
  3. Add Component > Rigidbody 2D. Set Gravity Scale to 3, Collision Detection to Continuous, Interpolate to Interpolate, and under Constraints tick Freeze Rotation Z so it can't tip over.
  4. Add Component > Capsule Collider 2D, which sizes itself to the sprite.
  5. Create > 2D > Physics Material 2D in Assets, named NoFriction, with Friction 0. Drag it into the collider's Material slot.

Press Play: the player drops onto the floor and stays upright. Gravity Scale 3 gives the snappy falls platformers usually have, and zero friction stops walls from pinning you in mid-air.

Right-click Player and choose Create Empty to add a child named GroundCheck at position (0, -1, 0). The Capsule shape is 2 units tall, so -1 in local space is exactly its bottom. The script will ask whether anything on the Ground layer overlaps a small circle there.

#Step 4: Running

Create PlayerController in Assets/Scripts and attach it to Player:

Update stores the input in a field, and FixedUpdate turns it into velocity on the physics clock. Only x is replaced: keeping rb.linearVelocity.y lets gravity work, and setting it to 0 would make the player float. Run into the Wall to check that it stops you.

#Step 5: Jumping, only from the ground

Add the jump fields and state below moveSpeed:

At the end of Update, remember a press:

And replace FixedUpdate:

Physics2D.OverlapCircle returns the first collider on the given layers inside the circle, or null. jumpQueued carries the one-frame press from Update to the next physics step, so no press is lost; it's cleared every step, so a mid-air press is dropped (the practice set improves that).

#Step 6: Face the way you run, and see the ground check

Add Module 3's facing method, called as FaceDirection(moveInput); at the end of Update, plus a gizmo that draws the ground check:

Press Play with Player selected and watch the circle turn red in the air and green on landing.

⚠️ The player can jump forever in mid-air

#Step 7: Saws send you back to the start

Add a respawn component to Player:

A respawn is a deliberate teleport, the one time setting the Transform directly is right, and clearing the velocity stops the player arriving with the speed it died with. Now the payoff from Module 2. Create a Hazard script:

Open Saw.prefab in Prefab Mode and, on its root, add a Circle Collider 2D with Is Trigger ticked plus the Hazard component. Back in the scene, every saw, bobbing variants included, is now dangerous.

#Step 8: Coins

Make a yellow Circle named Coin, scale (0.5, 0.5, 1), with a trigger Circle Collider 2D and the Coin script from the Notes. Make it a prefab and place five, including one in a risky spot near a bobbing saw. Saws and coins need no Rigidbody 2D, because the player's Dynamic body is the one in each pair. Module 5 upgrades Coin and Hazard with score, sound, and health, so keep these file names.

#Step 9: A Cinemachine follow camera

  1. In Window > Package Management > Package Manager, choose Unity Registry, find Cinemachine, and click Install.
  2. Click empty space in the Hierarchy so nothing is selected, then choose GameObject > Cinemachine > Targeted Cameras > 2D Camera. This creates a Cinemachine Camera with a Position Composer and adds a Cinemachine Brain to the Main Camera.
  3. Drag Player into the new camera's Tracking Target field.
  4. Under Lens, set Orthographic Size to 6.
  5. On the Position Composer, set Damping to 0.5 for X and 0.75 for Y, turn on Dead Zone, and set its size to about 0.15 wide by 0.25 tall.

Press Play. The camera trails the player slightly, and small steps inside the dead zone don't move it. The Main Camera's Transform is now driven by the Brain, so make camera changes on the Cinemachine Camera.

#Step 10: Keep the camera inside the level

At the left end the camera shows empty space. Create an empty CameraBounds at (10, 3.5, 0) with a Box Collider 2D of Size (41, 14) and Is Trigger ticked. Keep it on Default: ground checks detect triggers too, so on Ground it would make the player "grounded" everywhere.

On the Cinemachine Camera, use Add Extension to add Cinemachine Confiner 2D, and drag CameraBounds into Bounding Shape 2D. The camera now stops at the edges. If you resize the bounds later, click Invalidate Bounding Shape Cache on the confiner.

#The finished controller

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is the jump press stored in jumpQueued instead of jumping directly inside Update?

  • Update catches every press; FixedUpdate applies it in step with physics.

  • It works anywhere; the problem is that FixedUpdate doesn't run every frame.

  • At most it's one physics step, about 0.02 seconds; the reason is reliability, not feel.

Show answer

A. Update catches every press; FixedUpdate applies it in step with physics.

2You made the saws dangerous by editing Saw.prefab. What would have happened with twelve independent copy-pasted saws?

  • Independent copies don't share edits.

  • That's Module 2's drift problem; the prefab let one edit reach every saw.

  • Restarting doesn't link independent objects.

Show answer

B. That's Module 2's drift problem; the prefab let one edit reach every saw.

3Why must CameraBounds stay off the Ground layer?

  • The confiner reads whatever collider you assign, on any layer.

  • Physics queries include triggers by default, and the player is always inside the bounds.

Show answer

B. Physics queries include triggers by default, and the player is always inside the bounds.

Key takeaways

  • The player is a Dynamic Rigidbody 2D with a capsule, zero friction, Continuous detection, interpolation, and frozen rotation.
  • Read input in Update; in FixedUpdate, replace x velocity and keep y unless jumping.
  • Ground checks are an OverlapCircle at the feet with a LayerMask that excludes the player.
  • A Cinemachine 2D Camera with damping, a dead zone, and a Confiner 2D follows smoothly and stays in the level.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Set Lookahead Time to about 0.3 with Lookahead Ignore Y ticked, so the camera leads your running direction without bobbing on jumps.
  • Build a moving platform from a Kinematic Rigidbody 2D moved with rb.MovePosition in FixedUpdate, and see what happens to a player standing on it.

#Further reading

  • Cinemachine Confiner 2D (opens in a new tab): how the bounds are computed and cached, and what the damping and slowing distance settings do.
  • Rigidbody2D.interpolation (opens in a new tab): what interpolation and extrapolation do and when each one fits.

What you'll learn

  • Predict which physics events fire for a given pair of objects.
  • Make jumps feel responsive with variable height, coyote time, and a jump buffer.
  • See tunneling happen and fix it with Continuous collision detection.
  • Use layers and the Layer Collision Matrix to control exactly what touches what.
  • Change a Cinemachine camera from a script, gently.

Every exercise builds on SampleScene and PlayerController from the build-along. Commit (or copy the script) before each one, so you can always get back to a version that works.

#Warm-up: which event fires?

For each pair, decide whether Unity calls OnCollisionEnter2D, OnTriggerEnter2D, or nothing.

Pair Your prediction
Player (Dynamic body, capsule) lands on Ground (Box Collider 2D, no body)
Player touches a Coin (trigger, no body)
A Coin overlaps a Saw (both triggers, no bodies)
A falling crate (Dynamic body, box) hits a Saw (trigger, no body)

Answers: collision; trigger; nothing (neither has a Rigidbody 2D); trigger, where Hazard sees the crate isn't tagged Player and ignores it.

#Exercise 1: Falling off the world

Split Ground into two pieces with a 3-unit gap between them, somewhere past the first saws. Now make falling into the gap send the player back to the start. Try to do it without writing any new code.

Sample result: you walk into the gap, fall for a moment, and reappear at the spawn point with no velocity.

Need a hint?

What does Hazard actually check? It doesn't care what shape the trigger is or whether it looks like a saw.

Show solution

Create an empty KillZone at (10, -9, 0) with a Box Collider 2D of Size (60, 2), tick Is Trigger, and add the existing Hazard component. Hazard only asks "did the Player enter my trigger?", so it works for saws, pits, or lava. Keep the zone below the camera bounds so players never see it.

#Exercise 2: Hold to jump higher

In most platformers, tapping jump gives a small hop and holding it gives a full jump. Add this to PlayerController: if Space is released while the player is still rising, cut the upward velocity in half.

Sample result: a quick tap clears about a quarter of the height of a held jump; a held jump still reaches about 2.45 units.

Need a hint?

Releasing is a one-frame event, just like pressing, so detect it in Update with wasReleasedThisFrame and act on it in FixedUpdate. Only cut while velocity.y > 0, or releasing during a fall would slow the fall.

Show solution

In Update, after the jump-press line:

In FixedUpdate, right after the line that sets velocity.y = jumpSpeed:

Height grows with the square of launch speed, so half the speed gives a quarter of the height. Jumping before cutting means even a tap shorter than one physics step still gives a small hop.

#Exercise 3: Coyote time

Players often press jump a moment after running off a ledge, and the game ignores them because they're no longer grounded. Add coyote time: the player may still jump for 0.1 seconds after leaving the ground.

Sample result: run off Platform B and press Space just after the edge. The player jumps instead of falling.

Need a hint?

Keep a coyoteTimer. In FixedUpdate, refill it to 0.1 while grounded, and count it down with Time.fixedDeltaTime otherwise. Jump when the timer is above zero instead of when isGrounded is true, and empty the timer when you jump.

Show solution

In FixedUpdate:

Emptying coyoteTimer on a jump stops a second press in the next 0.1 seconds from jumping again in mid-air.

#Exercise 4: A jump buffer

The opposite problem: the player presses jump a moment before landing, the press is dropped, and the player lands without jumping. Replace jumpQueued with a jump buffer that remembers a press for 0.1 seconds. Keep coyote time working.

Sample result: tap Space just before touching down and the player bounces straight back up.

Need a hint?

Instead of a bool that's cleared every physics step, store a jumpBufferTimer. Set it to 0.1 when Space is pressed, count it down every frame in Update, and jump in FixedUpdate when both timers are above zero. Then empty both.

Counting down before recording the press gives each press the full 0.1 seconds. Coyote time forgives pressing late; the buffer forgives pressing early.

#Exercise 5: Watch a bullet tunnel

Build a test: a thin wall (a Square scaled to (0.2, 4, 1) with a Box Collider 2D) and, 5.5 units to its left, a Cannon that fires a bullet when you press F. The bullet is a small Circle (scale 0.2) with a Rigidbody 2D (Gravity Scale 0, Collision Detection Discrete), a Circle Collider 2D, and a script that logs "Hit" and destroys the bullet when it collides. Fire ten shots at 60 units per second and count the hits, then switch the bullet prefab to Continuous and count again.

Sample result:

Need a hint?

Make the prefab field a Rigidbody2D instead of a GameObject. Then Instantiate hands back the new bullet's Rigidbody 2D directly, and you can set its linearVelocity on the next line.

Show solution

At 60 units per second each step moves 1.2 units. From 5.5 units away the steps land at 4.8 and 6.0, either side of the wall, so Discrete never sees an overlap. Move the cannon 0.3 units and it might hit every time, which is exactly why Discrete can't be trusted for fast objects. Continuous sweeps between steps, so every shot connects.

#Exercise 6: Crates, and who ignores whom

Add a few crates (brown Squares with a Dynamic Rigidbody 2D and a Box Collider 2D). The design rules:

  1. The player can push crates, stand on them, and jump off them.
  2. Crates fall through saws and coins without setting them off or being destroyed.
  3. Saws still hurt the player, and coins can still be collected.
Need a hint?

Right now the player, saws, and coins all share the Default layer, so you can't separate them in the matrix. Give the player its own layer. Then decide which boxes to untick in Edit > Project Settings > Physics 2D, on the Layer Collision Matrix tab, and what the player's Ground Layer mask should contain.

Show solution

Create two layers, Player and Crate. Put the player on Player (when Unity asks whether to change its children too, say yes) and the crates on Crate. Saws and coins stay on Default.

In the Layer Collision Matrix, untick Crate / Default. Leave Crate / Player, Crate / Ground, and Crate / Crate ticked. Leave Player / Default ticked, so the player still triggers saws and coins.

Set the player's Ground Layer to Ground and Crate so crates can be jumped from, but never Player, or the check would find the player's own collider. Rule 2 works because an unticked pair never touches, so no trigger event is generated.

#Challenge: A zoom-out zone

Make a CameraZoomZone: a wide trigger between Platform A and the Wall. While the player is inside, the camera eases from Orthographic Size 6 out to 7 at about 1.5 units per second, and eases back when they leave. Keep it gradual, since sudden framing jumps are uncomfortable. The confiner caches its area per lens size, so call CinemachineConfiner2D.InvalidateLensCache() whenever the size changes.

Need a hint?

Add using Unity.Cinemachine; to reach CinemachineCamera. Its lens is a public field, so cinemachineCamera.Lens.OrthographicSize can be read and assigned directly. Track whether the player is inside with OnTriggerEnter2D and OnTriggerExit2D, and move the size with Mathf.MoveTowards in Update. Why 7 and not 10? Check the height of CameraBounds.

Show solution

Put it on an empty ZoomZone with a large trigger Box Collider 2D on Default, and drag the Cinemachine Camera into both slots. The Approximately check leaves the lens and cache alone once the zoom settles.

CameraBounds is 14 units tall, and size 7 shows exactly 14 units. Size 10 would show 20, more than the bounds hold, so the confiner couldn't keep the view inside. Make the bounds taller before zooming further.

What you'll learn

  • Build an Animator Controller from states, transitions, and parameters, and drive it from C# with SetFloat, SetBool, and SetTrigger.
  • Put score and health on screen with a Canvas, a Canvas Scaler, and TextMeshPro text.
  • Play looping music and overlapping sound effects with AudioSource and PlayOneShot.
  • Connect gameplay to feedback with C# events, so a health script never needs to know the HUD exists.

Hand your game to a friend and watch them play. They brush a spike, lose a heart, and keep walking, because the only thing that changed was a number in an Inspector they can't see. Ten seconds later they "die out of nowhere" and put the controller down. The code worked perfectly. The game just never told them anything.

Players find out what happened through three channels: what moves, what they can read, and what they hear. Anything that matters should reach them through at least two.

Event Animation UI Audio
Took damage Hurt pose, sprite flashes Health bar drops Short hit sound
Picked up a coin Coin disappears Score ticks up Bright chime
Low on health (optional) slower walk Bar turns red Heartbeat loop
Paused Everything freezes Pause panel appears Music pauses

Below is how each channel works in Unity 6. The build-along that follows wires all three into your game.

#Clips hold the frames; the Animator Controller picks which clip plays

Think of a flipbook for every action (idle, run, jump, hurt) plus a referee who decides which flipbook is open right now. The flipbooks are Animation Clips. The referee is an Animator Controller.

More precisely:

  • An Animation Clip (.anim file) stores keyframes over time. In a 2D sprite clip, each keyframe swaps the Sprite shown by the SpriteRenderer.
  • An Animator Controller (.controller file) is a state machine. Each state plays one clip. Transitions are arrows between states, and each arrow has conditions.
  • Conditions are written in terms of parameters, which come in four types: Float, Int, Bool, and Trigger. A Trigger is a Bool that switches itself off as soon as a transition uses it.
  • The Animator component on your Player runs the controller every frame.

To make the first clip, select the Player, open Window > Animation > Animation, click Create, and save the clip as Idle.anim. Unity creates the clip, creates an Animator Controller beside it, and adds an Animator component to the Player in one step. Drag the idle frames from the Project window onto the timeline. For the other actions, open the clip dropdown at the top left of the Animation window and choose Create New Clip....

Then open Window > Animation > Animator to see the controller as a graph. Here is the one this module builds:

Add the parameters in the Parameters tab on the left of the Animator window (the + button). Right-click a state and choose Make Transition to draw an arrow, then click the arrow to edit it in the Inspector.

Two transition settings decide whether your animation feels responsive or sluggish:

  • Has Exit Time makes the transition wait until the current clip reaches its Exit Time (1 means "the end of the clip"). That's right for Hurt → Idle, which should play the whole hurt clip and then return. It's wrong for Idle → Run, where the player pressed a key and expects to see running now. Untick it for every transition that a parameter controls.
  • Transition Duration, under Settings, blends two clips over time. Sprite frames can't be blended halfway, so set it to 0 for crisp 2D art.

#Feeding parameters from C#

The Animator only knows what you tell it. A small script reads the Rigidbody2D and copies the facts into parameters every frame:

Three lines deserve a closer look. Mathf.Abs matters because running left gives a negative speed, and the condition "Speed above 0.1" would never be true for it. Animator.StringToHash turns each parameter name into an integer once, so the name is typed in exactly one place and Unity doesn't compare strings every frame. The normal-angle filter counts only surfaces under the player's feet as ground: touching a wall gives a sideways normal (near 0° or 180°), which is filtered out.

This script reads the movement and never changes it. Your PlayerController from Module 4 already exposes its ground check as the IsGrounded property, so read that instead of checking twice.

Press Play with the Animator window open. The current state shows a blue progress bar, and the Parameters tab updates live, which is the fastest way to see why a transition isn't firing.

#A Canvas that fits every screen

UI lives on a sheet of glass in front of the camera, not in the game world. In Unity's built-in UI system that glass is a Canvas. With Render Mode set to Screen Space - Overlay (the default), the Canvas is drawn on top of everything in screen pixels, no matter where the camera goes.

Right-click in the Hierarchy and choose UI > Text - TextMeshPro. Unity creates a Canvas, an EventSystem, and a Text (TMP) object. The first time, a TMP Importer window asks to import the essential resources; click Import TMP Essentials.

Now the trap. The Canvas Scaler starts in Constant Pixel Size mode, so a 36-pixel score looks fine at 1920 × 1080, tiny on a 4K monitor, and huge in a small browser window. Select the Canvas and change its Canvas Scaler:

  • UI Scale Mode: Scale With Screen Size
  • Reference Resolution: 1920 × 1080
  • Screen Match Mode: Match Width Or Height, with Match at 0.5

You now design the HUD once at 1080p, and Unity scales it to the real screen. Then anchor each element to the corner it belongs to. In the Rect Transform, click the anchor presets square and hold Alt (Option on a Mac) while you pick top-left, so the score moves to that corner as well as anchoring there.

🧪 Try it yourself

In the Game view, open the aspect dropdown (it says something like "Free Aspect" or "Full HD") and switch between a wide and a tall size. With Scale With Screen Size, the score stays the same size relative to the screen and stays in its corner.

Changing the text from code takes one field and one assignment:

#Sound: one listener, many sources

Unity's audio works like a room with one microphone and many speakers. The microphone is the Audio Listener, already on the Main Camera. Each speaker is an Audio Source component, and the sound file it plays is an AudioClip.

The Audio Source settings you'll use most:

  • Play On Awake starts the clip when the object appears. Good for music, bad for a hurt sound.
  • Loop repeats the clip. Again, music yes, effects no.
  • Spatial Blend at 0 means 2D: the sound ignores where things are in the scene. Leave it at 0 for most 2D games.

There are two ways to play an effect, and the difference shows up the moment the player grabs two coins quickly:

Play() restarts the one clip the source owns. PlayOneShot doesn't cancel clips that are already playing, so ten quick coins give ten overlapping chimes. The random pitch keeps repeated sounds from sounding like a machine gun. Pitch belongs to the whole source, though, so it also bends anything else that source is playing.

Give music its own Audio Source with Play On Awake and Loop ticked and Volume around 0.4, so you can change music and effects separately.

#Events keep gameplay and feedback apart

Here's the design mistake almost everyone makes first: the health script calls the health bar, the animator, the sound player, and the camera shake directly. Each new piece of feedback means editing the health script, and the health script breaks in any scene without a HUD.

The fix is for health to announce "I changed" and let anything that cares listen. In C# that announcement is an event:

And one listener:

Changed?.Invoke(...) calls every subscriber, and the ?. means "do nothing if nobody subscribed" instead of throwing. The listener subscribes in OnEnable and unsubscribes in OnDisable, so a destroyed HUD never gets called. It draws the starting value in Start because Unity runs every object's Awake before any Start, so health.Current is already set by then.

⚠️ Watch out

Parameter names must match exactly. animator.SetFloat("speed", 2f) when the parameter is called Speed doesn't throw an error. It logs the warning Parameter 'speed' does not exist. and nothing animates. Declaring each hash once with Animator.StringToHash keeps the name in a single place.

⚠️ Watch out

An Any State transition can fire every frame. Any State → Jump with the condition "Grounded is false" restarts Jump on every frame you're in the air, so the clip freezes on its first frame. Untick Can Transition To Self on that transition, or use a Trigger, which switches itself off after one use.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The Idle → Run transition still has Has Exit Time ticked with Exit Time 1, and the Idle clip is 1 second long. The player presses right halfway through the Idle loop. What happens?

  • It would with Has Exit Time unticked. With it ticked, the transition also waits for the exit time.

  • The transition can only fire when Idle reaches the end of its loop, so the sprite keeps idling while the body moves.

  • It does start, just late: once the Idle clip reaches 100%, the Speed condition is checked and passes.

Show answer

B. The transition can only fire when Idle reaches the end of its loop, so the sprite keeps idling while the body moves.

2Your coin script runs source.clip = coinClip; source.Play();. The player grabs three coins within 0.2 seconds. What does the player hear?

  • That's what PlayOneShot gives you. Play owns a single clip and restarts it.

  • Each Play() call restarts the same clip from the beginning.

  • Play() doesn't skip when a clip is playing; it restarts it.

Show answer

B. Each Play() call restarts the same clip from the beginning.

3You want the Hurt animation to play once per hit, then return to Idle. Which parameter type should the Any State → Hurt transition use?

  • A Bool stays true until your code clears it, so Any State keeps re-entering Hurt.

  • A Float can work with a condition, but you'd still need to reset it, which is exactly what a Trigger does for you.

  • The transition uses the trigger and the trigger switches itself off, so one hit gives one Hurt.

Show answer

C. The transition uses the trigger and the trigger switches itself off, so one hit gives one Hurt.

4The Canvas Scaler is left on Constant Pixel Size. You designed a 48-pixel score at 1920 × 1080. How does it look on a 3840 × 2160 monitor?

  • Constant Pixel Size keeps 48 real pixels, and the screen now has twice as many.

  • That's what Scale With Screen Size does, by scaling everything by 2.

  • Pixels don't grow on a bigger screen; they shrink relative to it.

Show answer

A. Constant Pixel Size keeps 48 real pixels, and the screen now has twice as many.

Key takeaways

  • Clips hold frames; the Animator Controller is a state machine whose transitions check parameters you set from code.
  • Untick Has Exit Time on input-driven transitions, and set Transition Duration to 0 for sprite art.
  • Use Scale With Screen Size on the Canvas Scaler and anchor each UI element to its corner.
  • PlayOneShot layers sounds; Play restarts the one clip a source owns.
  • Gameplay scripts raise events, and feedback scripts subscribe in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable.

#Further reading

  • Animation transitions (opens in a new tab): every transition setting, including Exit Time and interruption, with the graph explained.
  • Canvas Scaler (opens in a new tab): the three scale modes and what Match does between width and height.
  • Audio Source (opens in a new tab): the full property list, including priority and the 3D sound settings you'll want for a 3D game.

What you'll learn

  • Animate the player with Idle, Run, and Hurt states driven by parameters.
  • Build a scaled HUD with a TextMeshPro score and a Slider health bar.
  • Make coins, spikes, and a shared sound player that layers effects with PlayOneShot.
  • Give damage three kinds of feedback (a flash, a Hurt animation, and a sound) through one Health event.
  • Freeze the game on death and restart it from a UI Button.

Your player can already run, jump, and collide with the level. By the end of this build the game will also explain itself: coins chime and raise a score in the corner, spikes knock the player upward, the sprite flashes red while a hurt pose plays, the health bar drops, and at zero health a Game Over panel offers a Restart button.

Here's every script you'll write and who talks to whom:

#Step 1: Bring in art and sound you're allowed to use

You need a few animation frames, a coin, a spike, and three or four sounds. Two free sources with no strings attached:

  • Kenney's Pixel Platformer (opens in a new tab) has characters, coins, and spikes. Kenney's assets are released as CC0, so you can use them in anything without credit (credit is still polite).
  • sfxr.me (opens in a new tab) generates retro sound effects in the browser. Click Pickup/Coin or Hit/Hurt until you like one, then export it as a WAV.

Create folders Art, Audio, and Scripts in your Assets. Drag the files in. For pixel art, select the sprite sheet and set these in the Inspector, then click Apply:

  • Sprite Mode: Multiple
  • Pixels Per Unit: the size of one tile in the pack, so one tile is one Unity unit
  • Filter Mode: Point (no filter), which keeps the pixels sharp
  • Compression: None

Click Open Sprite Editor, choose Slice > Grid By Cell Size, enter the frame size, click Slice, then Apply. Each frame becomes its own sprite under the sheet.

#Step 2: Idle, Run, and Hurt in the Animator

Select the Player, open Window > Animation > Animation, click Create, and save Idle.anim in Art/Animations. Drag the idle frames onto the timeline. Use the clip dropdown's Create New Clip... to make Run.anim and Hurt.anim the same way. Open the Hurt clip and untick Loop Time in its Inspector, so it plays once.

In Window > Animation > Animator, add three parameters: Speed (Float), Grounded (Bool), and Hurt (Trigger). Then make these transitions:

From → To Has Exit Time Transition Duration Condition
Idle → Run off 0 Speed Greater 0.1
Run → Idle off 0 Speed Less 0.1
Any State → Hurt off 0 Hurt (and untick Can Transition To Self)
Hurt → Idle on, Exit Time 1 0 none

Add the PlayerAnimation script from the Notes lesson to the Player and set Ground Layers to the layer your level uses. Press Play and run back and forth. The Animator window should show the blue progress bar jumping between Idle and Run as you start and stop. If you made a Jump clip, add it with the Grounded transitions from the Notes diagram.

#Step 3: A Canvas that scales, with a score in the corner

Right-click in the Hierarchy, choose UI > Text - TextMeshPro, and import TMP Essentials if Unity asks. Rename the Canvas to HUD and the text to ScoreText.

On the HUD's Canvas Scaler, set UI Scale Mode to Scale With Screen Size, Reference Resolution to 1920 × 1080, and Match to 0.5. On ScoreText, open the anchor presets, hold Alt (Option on a Mac), and click top-left. Set Pos X to 40, Pos Y to -40, the font size to 48, and the text to Score: 0.

📝 Note

If the Console warns about the EventSystem using the old input module, select EventSystem in the Hierarchy and click Replace with InputSystemUIInputModule. Buttons won't respond to clicks until the EventSystem uses the Input System.

#Step 4: A score keeper, a label, and coins

The score needs one owner. Create an empty GameObject called GameSystems and add this script:

Instance lets a coin find the score keeper without an Inspector reference. That matters because the coin will be a prefab, and a prefab asset can't hold references to objects in a scene.

Add this label script to ScoreText and drag ScoreText into its Label slot:

It subscribes in Start rather than OnEnable, because Start is guaranteed to run after ScoreKeeper.Awake has set Instance.

Now the coin. Drag a coin sprite into the scene, add a Circle Collider 2D, and tick Is Trigger. Make sure your Player's Tag is set to Player. Add:

The collected flag is there because a player with two colliders (a body and a feet box, say) can enter the trigger twice in the same physics step, and Destroy doesn't take effect until the end of the frame. Without it, one coin sometimes scores 20.

Drag the coin from the Hierarchy into a Prefabs folder to make it a prefab, then place several. It won't compile until the next step adds SoundPlayer.

#Step 5: One sound player for every effect

If the coin played its sound from its own Audio Source, Destroy(gameObject) would delete the source in the same frame and the sound would stop almost before it started. Instead, every effect goes through one long-lived source. Add an Audio Source to GameSystems, untick Play On Awake, and add:

Select the coin prefab and drag your coin WAV into Pickup Sound. For music, create another empty object called Music, add an Audio Source, assign a looping track, and tick Play On Awake and Loop with Volume at 0.4.

Press Play and grab coins. The score climbs by 10 per coin, and the chime layers when you grab two quickly.

#Step 6: Health with a safety window, spikes, and a health bar

Taking damage every physics step while touching a spike would empty the bar in a blink. Real games give a short window of invulnerability after each hit. This Health extends the Notes version with that window and a separate Damaged event. Add it to the Player (if your Module 4 work already has a health script, merge these events into it):

Spikes (and the saw blades from Module 2) get a trigger collider and this script. It damages anything with a Health and bounces it upward so the player isn't left standing in the hazard:

For the bar, right-click the HUD and choose UI > Slider. Name it HealthBar and anchor it top-right. Delete its child Handle Slide Area, and on the Slider component untick Interactable and tick Whole Numbers. Color the child Fill image red. Then add:

Drag the Player (from the Hierarchy, not the Project window) into Health and the slider into Slider. Walk into the spikes: the bar drops one step, you bounce, and touching them again within a second does nothing.

#Step 7: Flash, hurt pose, sound, and game over

The hurt feedback listens to Damaged. The flashing lasts 0.8 seconds, inside the 1-second safety window, so it also tells the player "you can't be hit right now." It blinks two and a half times per second, under the limit of three flashes per second from the safety notes in Module 1.

Add it to the Player and fill its slots from the Player's own components.

For game over, right-click the HUD and add UI > Panel, name it GameOverPanel, and give it a Text (TMP) child saying "Game Over" and a UI > Button - TextMeshPro child labeled "Restart". Add this script to the HUD object, not to the panel: a script on an inactive object never runs OnEnable, so it would never hear the Died event.

Select the Restart button, find On Click () on its Button component, click +, drag the HUD into the object slot, and choose GameOverScreen > Restart. Restarting reloads the scene by its build index, so the scene must be listed in File > Build Profiles under Scene List (new projects already include SampleScene; use Add Open Scenes if yours isn't there).

Play through: grab coins, hit spikes five times, and press Restart. Expected behavior:

#The finished scene

Notice what Health doesn't reference: no HUD, no sound, no animator. Delete the HUD and the game still runs; the damage just stops being shown.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the coin play its sound through SoundPlayer instead of an Audio Source on the coin itself?

  • It works on any Audio Source; the name doesn't matter.

  • A long-lived source keeps playing after the coin is gone.

  • Prefabs can have any component. The problem is the coin's lifetime, not its type.

Show answer

B. A long-lived source keeps playing after the coin is gone.

2GameOverScreen sits on the HUD, not on GameOverPanel. What would go wrong if it were on the panel?

  • Scripts on inactive GameObjects don't run their lifecycle methods until the object is activated.

  • Nothing duplicates. The panel would simply never appear.

  • Any script can set Time.timeScale. The issue is that the script never hears the event.

Show answer

A. Scripts on inactive GameObjects don't run their lifecycle methods until the object is activated.

3You remove the invulnerableUntil check from Health. The Hazard still uses OnTriggerEnter2D. What changes most noticeably?

  • Enter fires once per touch, but a second spike or an enemy touching you right after the first hit would also land.

  • The safety window is what stops back-to-back hits and gives the flash its meaning.

  • The bar still updates; it may just drop several steps at once.

Show answer

B. The safety window is what stops back-to-back hits and gives the flash its meaning.

Key takeaways

  • A single owner (ScoreKeeper, Health) holds each value and raises an event when it changes.
  • Effects play through a long-lived SoundPlayer, so destroying the object that caused a sound doesn't silence it.
  • A short invulnerability window plus a flash turns "touching spikes" into one clear, readable hit.
  • A script that must hear an event can't live on an object that starts inactive.
  • Time.timeScale = 0 freezes physics and animation; set it back to 1 before reloading a scene.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Replace the bar with a row of heart icons: one Image per heart, switched on or off in Show.
  • Make the score count up over half a second instead of jumping, using a coroutine.
  • Add a short hit pause: set Time.timeScale to 0.05 for 0.06 seconds of unscaled time (WaitForSecondsRealtime) when the player is hit.
  • Add a Heal pickup that calls health.Heal(1) and plays its own sound.

#Further reading

  • Slider (opens in a new tab): every Slider property, including Direction for vertical bars.
  • TextMesh Pro in Unity 6 (opens in a new tab): fonts, rich text tags, and the TMP settings asset.
  • Coroutines (opens in a new tab): how yield return new WaitForSeconds pauses a method without freezing the game.

What you'll learn

  • Extend an Animator Controller with a new state and the parameter that drives it.
  • Read and fix two errors that every Unity programmer meets.
  • Format time for a HUD and change its color as a warning.
  • Rate-limit and vary sound effects, and start or stop a loop from an event.
  • Pause the game with Time.timeScale while the menu stays usable.

#Warm-up: predict the animation

A teammate wrote this line and says "running right works, but running left stays in Idle." The Idle → Run condition is Speed Greater 0.1.

Before reading on, decide why. Running left gives a negative x velocity such as -5, and -5 is not greater than 0.1, so the transition never fires. The fix is Mathf.Abs(rb.linearVelocity.x): the Animator needs "how fast," and the sprite's flipX already handles "which way."

#Exercise 1: Add a Fall state

Right now the player shows the Jump clip all the way up and all the way down. Add a Fall clip that plays while moving downward in the air, and a VerticalSpeed Float parameter that drives it.

Expected behavior:

Need a hint?

The top of a jump is the moment vertical velocity goes from positive to negative. You need one transition into Fall and one out of it, and neither should wait for an exit time.

Show solution

Add VerticalSpeed (Float) in the Parameters tab, then make two transitions, both with Has Exit Time off and Transition Duration 0:

From → To Conditions
Jump → Fall VerticalSpeed Less -0.1
Fall → Idle Grounded true

In PlayerAnimation, add a hash and one line in Update:

Here you want the sign, so there's no Mathf.Abs. The small -0.1 margin stops Fall from flickering on for a single frame when the player brushes a ledge. If the player walks off a ledge without jumping, add Run → Fall with "Grounded false" and "VerticalSpeed Less -0.1" too.

#Exercise 2: Read the compiler error

This script won't compile:

The Console says:

Explain the error and give two fixes.

Need a hint?

Look at the two using lines. Each namespace contains a type called Random.

Show solution

using System; (needed for Action) brings in System.Random, and using UnityEngine; brings in UnityEngine.Random. The compiler refuses to guess which one you mean. Either fix works:

Notice that Random.Range(0, steps.Length) with whole numbers never returns steps.Length: the int version excludes the maximum, which is exactly right for array indexes.

#Exercise 3: A countdown timer that turns red

Show a 90-second countdown in the top-center of the HUD as m:ss. Under 10 seconds the text turns red. At zero, call health.TakeDamage(health.Max) so the existing game-over flow runs.

Sample output on screen:

Need a hint?

Count down a float with Time.deltaTime, but display a whole number of seconds. Rounding up with Mathf.CeilToInt means the display shows 0:00 only when time has really run out.

Show solution

Check the formatting rule quickly in Python before writing the C#:

The C# version does the same thing every frame:

{total % 60:00} pads the seconds to two digits. Because the timer uses Time.deltaTime, it stops on its own when the game-over screen sets Time.timeScale to 0. Updating the text every frame is fine here since the value really does change; for a cheaper version, only assign label.text when total changes.

#Exercise 4: Footsteps that don't sound robotic

Play a footstep every 0.3 seconds while the player is on the ground and moving faster than 0.5 units per second. Pick a random clip from an array each time.

Need a hint?

Keep a countdown float. Subtract Time.deltaTime each frame while walking; when it reaches zero, play a step and reset it to 0.3. Reuse the Grounded check you already have.

Show solution

Three or four clips plus the pitch variation in SoundPlayer is enough to stop the ear from spotting the repeat. Resetting to zero when the player stops makes the first step land on the first frame of movement, which feels connected to the input.

#Exercise 5: A heartbeat at low health

When health drops to 1, start a looping heartbeat sound. When the player heals above 1 (or the scene restarts), it stops. Use the Changed event, not Update.

Need a hint?

Give this script its own Audio Source with Loop ticked and Play On Awake unticked. AudioSource.isPlaying tells you whether it's already going, so you don't restart it on every hit.

Show solution

This is a case for Play() rather than PlayOneShot: there's one looping clip that you need to stop later, and Stop() controls the source's own clip. The current > 0 check silences the heartbeat on death so it doesn't play over the Game Over panel.

#Exercise 6: A pause menu that still works while paused

Pressing Escape shows a PausePanel with a Resume button and freezes the game. Pressing Escape again, or clicking Resume, unfreezes it. Sound effects and music should pause too.

Need a hint?

Time.timeScale = 0 stops physics and anything that uses Time.deltaTime, but Update still runs, so you can still read the keyboard. AudioListener.pause pauses every Audio Source at once. Hook Resume to a public method through the button's On Click () list.

Show solution

Put it on the HUD (an always-active object), drag PausePanel into Panel, and point the Resume button's On Click at PauseMenu.Resume. UI buttons keep working at a time scale of 0 because the EventSystem doesn't depend on game time. If you animate the pause panel, set that Animator's Update Mode to Unscaled Time, or it will freeze along with everything else. And don't let Escape unpause the Game Over screen: check that the player is alive before toggling.

#Challenge: Feedback everyone can perceive

Some players can't hear your sounds, can't tell red from green, or get headaches from flashing. Add a small Options panel (reachable from the pause menu) with:

  1. A Reduce flashing toggle. When it's on, HurtFeedback tints the sprite once for 0.5 seconds instead of blinking.
  2. A Captions toggle. When it's on, important sounds also show a short text line near the bottom of the screen for 1.5 seconds, such as [hit], [coin], or [heartbeat].
  3. A health bar that doesn't rely on color alone: show the number (3/5) beside the bar.

Keep the option values in one GameOptions script with static fields for now. In Module 7 you'll save them with PlayerPrefs so they survive a restart.

Need a hint?

A UI Toggle has an onValueChanged event that passes the new bool. For captions, give SoundPlayer.Play an optional caption string and let a CaptionLabel script subscribe to a static event that SoundPlayer raises.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write an enemy as an enum of states with a switch, and name the rule that leaves each state.
  • Move along waypoints with Vector2.MoveTowards and Rigidbody2D.MovePosition.
  • Sense the player with a distance check, a Physics2D.Linecast, and separate detect and lose radii.
  • Spawn enemies with Instantiate, cap how many exist, and hand each one the scene references it needs.
  • Plan a level as a sequence that teaches, tests, and then twists one mechanic.

The first enemy most people write is one line: every frame, move toward the player. Play it and three things go wrong. It glues itself to the wall between you and it. It's either unbeatable or trivially dodged, with nothing in between. And it gives no warning, so getting hit feels random.

The level around it often has the same problem. Spikes appear in the first room, a moving platform over spikes in the second, and nothing ever showed the player what spikes do when failure was cheap. Both problems have the same fix: decide what the player should notice, and when.

#An enemy is a few states and the rules for switching

Watch a guard in a stealth game. It walks a route. When it spots you it runs at you. When you break line of sight it goes to where it last saw you, looks around, and gives up. Each of those is a state: one behavior plus the rules that end it.

In C#, an enum names the states and a switch runs the current one:

Why not two Bools, isChasing and isSearching? Because nothing stops both from being true, and then which behavior runs depends on which if you happened to write first. An enum can hold exactly one value, so impossible combinations can't happen. The code runs in FixedUpdate because the enemy moves a Rigidbody2D, and physics moves happen on the physics clock.

#Patrol: follow a route of waypoints

A route is an array of empty GameObjects placed in the scene. The enemy moves toward the current one, and on arrival advances to the next:

Vector2.MoveTowards steps at most speed * Time.fixedDeltaTime toward the target and never overshoots, so the arrival check is guaranteed to pass eventually. % waypoints.Length wraps the index: with four waypoints it goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1. For a flying enemy, give the Rigidbody2D a Body Type of Kinematic. A kinematic body goes exactly where MovePosition puts it, ignores gravity, and still triggers collision events with the dynamic player.

You can see the radii while you tune them by drawing gizmos, which appear in the Scene view only:

#Sensing: distance, line of sight, and a gap between "see" and "lose"

Sensing has two checks, cheapest first. Is the player close enough? Then, is there a wall in between? Physics2D.Linecast answers the second by testing the straight segment between two points against colliders on the layers you choose:

A RaycastHit2D converts to true when it hit something, so !Physics2D.Linecast(...) reads as "nothing blocked the line."

Notice there are two radii. Patrol switches to Chase at 5, but Chase only gives up beyond 7. With a single radius, a player standing right at the edge makes the enemy flip between states every physics step, and it visibly jitters. The gap between the two thresholds is called hysteresis, and thermostats use it for the same reason. Step through the drone's decision with the player hovering around the edge:

Once the drone starts chasing at 4.9, wobbling between 4.8 and 5.3 doesn't matter; only moving past 7 ends the chase. Here's how many times the state flips with a single radius instead:

Four flips in eight frames with one radius, against two (start chasing, then give up) with hysteresis. At 50 physics steps a second, the single-radius drone shakes in place.

#Spawners: prefabs stamped out on a timer, with a cap

A spawner makes copies of a prefab while the game runs. Instantiate(prefab, position, rotation) returns the new copy. If the prefab field is typed as a component, such as EnemyAI, you get that component back directly:

That Setup call solves a problem you'll hit the first time you make an enemy prefab: its Player slot can't be filled. A prefab is an asset on disk, and assets can't point at objects inside one particular scene. The spawner lives in the scene, so it knows the player and hands the reference over at spawn time.

Every spawner also needs a cap (for example, "at most 3 alive"). Without one, a player who hides in a corner gets buried under an endless stream of enemies, and the frame rate goes with it.

#Difficulty is a handful of numbers

"Make it harder" is too vague to act on. Difficulty in an action game comes down to a few knobs: enemy speed, detect radius, how long the enemy warns before it acts, damage per hit, spawn interval, and the cap. Change one knob at a time, then playtest.

To ramp a knob over time, Unity's AnimationCurve gives you an editable graph in the Inspector:

This curve starts at 6 seconds between spawns and slides to 2 seconds by the two-minute mark. Click the curve in the Inspector to bend it: an easy first minute and a steep second one is a single drag.

#Levels that teach, test, and then twist

Unity builds 2D levels with Tilemaps. A Grid object holds one or more Tilemap layers, and you paint tiles onto them from the Tile Palette (Window > 2D > Tile Palette). Keep separate tilemaps for separate jobs: a Background with no collider, a Ground layer with a collider, and a Hazards layer whose collider is a trigger. The build-along sets all of this up.

The tools are the easy part. The hard part is deciding what goes where, and a widely used structure is to give each mechanic four beats:

For a patrolling drone, that might look like this. Teach: the player first sees the drone from a ledge, outside its detect radius, crossing an empty room. Test: its route crosses the only path, with a pillar to hide behind while it passes. Twist: two drones and a spike floor, so stopping to hide is no longer free. Conclude: a short stretch the player now handles easily, then the exit.

A few more principles to keep in mind:

  • One new idea per section. If a player dies to a spike-and-drone combination before seeing either alone, they learn nothing from it.
  • Show before it matters. Frame threats so the camera reveals them before they can reach the player; your Cinemachine setup from Module 4 helps here.
  • Use coins as signposts. A trail of coins says "go this way" without a word of text.
  • Pace tension with rest. Put a quiet stretch and a checkpoint before each twist, so a failure there doesn't repeat the easy parts.
  • Fit the space to the AI. A simple drone flies in straight lines. Give it an open room, and players read that room as "the drone's territory," which costs far less than writing pathfinding.

⚠️ Watch out

Waypoints parented to the enemy. If the waypoint objects are children of the drone, they move with it, so the drone chases a target that keeps moving away and drifts off forever. Put the waypoints under a separate Route object in the scene.

⚠️ Watch out

A line of sight that's always blocked. If sightBlockers includes the enemy's own layer (or Everything), the linecast starts inside the enemy's collider and hits it, so the enemy never sees anyone. Set the mask to just the layers that block sight, usually Ground.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A drone uses one radius of 5 for both "start chasing" and "stop chasing." The player stands about 5 units away. What does the drone do?

  • It would if the start and stop thresholds were different.

  • Small changes in distance cross the single threshold back and forth.

  • It does notice the player, many times a second, and then forgets again.

Show answer

B. Small changes in distance cross the single threshold back and forth.

2Your drone prefab has a Player field, but you can't drag the scene's Player into it while editing the prefab. Why?

  • Both show in the Inspector. Visibility isn't the problem.

  • The spawner, which lives in the scene, passes the reference in with Setup after Instantiate.

  • Transform fields serialize fine; that's how waypoints work.

Show answer

B. The spawner, which lives in the scene, passes the reference in with Setup after Instantiate.

3With four waypoints, index = (index + 1) % waypoints.Length; runs six times starting from 0. Which indexes does the drone visit?

  • Index 4 doesn't exist in a four-item array; % wraps it back to 0.

  • The remainder after dividing by 4 cycles through 0 to 3.

  • That would be clamping, not wrapping.

Show answer

B. The remainder after dividing by 4 cycles through 0 to 3.

4Where should the player first meet the drone?

  • A tense first meeting means the player learns the rules by dying.

  • They learn its route and range while failure is impossible, then get tested on it next.

  • Two unknown threats at once teach neither one.

Show answer

B. They learn its route and range while failure is impossible, then get tested on it next.

Key takeaways

  • An enemy is an enum of states, a switch that runs the current one, and an exit rule for each.
  • Vector2.MoveTowards plus MovePosition on a kinematic body gives exact, overshoot-free patrols.
  • Sense with a cheap distance check first, then a Linecast against the walls; use separate detect and lose radii.
  • Spawners need a cap, and they pass scene references to each prefab copy they create.
  • Give each mechanic a teach, test, twist, and conclude beat, and shape the space to fit what your AI can do.

#Further reading

  • State, from Game Programming Patterns (opens in a new tab): Robert Nystrom's free chapter on why enum state machines beat piles of Bools, and what to do when they grow.
  • Tilemaps in Unity 6 (opens in a new tab): grids, tilemap layers, and the Tile Palette.
  • Object.Instantiate (opens in a new tab): every overload, including spawning as a child of a parent Transform.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Paint Background, Ground, and Hazards tilemaps and give Ground a single merged collider.
  • Build a drone prefab that patrols, chases with line of sight, and searches before giving up.
  • Show the drone's state to the player with color and an alert sound.
  • Spawn drones from a capped spawner whose timing tightens over two minutes.
  • Lay out a short level that teaches, tests, and twists the drone.

By the end of this build you'll have a short, complete level. The player starts on a ledge and watches a drone sweep an empty room. Further on, the drone's route crosses the only path and a pillar offers cover. Then comes a room where drones keep arriving over a spike floor, and finally the exit. When a drone spots the player it turns red and beeps; when it loses them it turns yellow and drifts to where they were last seen.

#Step 1: Paint the level on three tilemaps

Right-click in the Hierarchy and choose 2D Object > Tilemap > Rectangular. Unity creates a Grid with one child Tilemap. Rename the child Ground, then right-click the Grid and add two more tilemaps the same way: Background and Hazards.

Open Window > 2D > Tile Palette. Create a new palette (save it in Art/Palettes), then drag your sliced tile sheet into the palette window and choose a folder such as Art/Tiles for the tile assets Unity generates. Each sprite becomes a paintable tile.

Before painting, check that the tile sheet's Pixels Per Unit equals the tile size in pixels. Then one tile fills exactly one Grid cell. If tiles look tiny with gaps between them, or huge and overlapping, that number is wrong.

Choose which tilemap you're painting on with the target dropdown at the top of the Tile Palette, pick the brush (B), and paint. Box Fill (U) is quicker for big floors and walls, and Erase (D) removes tiles. Paint the floor and walls on Ground, decoration on Background, and spikes on Hazards.

Set the drawing order on each tilemap's Tilemap Renderer: Order in Layer -10 for Background and 0 for Ground and Hazards. Set the Player's Sprite Renderer to 10 so it's drawn in front.

#Step 2: One merged collider for the ground, a trigger for the spikes

Select Ground and add a Tilemap Collider 2D. Every tile now has its own small box. That works, but the player can snag on the seams where boxes meet, so merge them:

  1. Add a Composite Collider 2D. Unity also adds a Rigidbody2D.
  2. Set that Rigidbody2D's Body Type to Static.
  3. On the Tilemap Collider 2D, set Composite Operation to Merge.

The green outline in the Scene view changes from a grid of squares to one smooth outline around each solid area. Set the Ground object's Layer to your Ground layer (the one your movement script and PlayerAnimation check).

Select Hazards, add a Tilemap Collider 2D, tick Is Trigger, and add the Hazard script from Module 5. Every spike tile now damages and bounces the player through one script.

#Step 3: The drone prefab and a route

Make the drone from any small sprite. Give it:

  • a Rigidbody2D with Body Type set to Kinematic,
  • a Circle Collider 2D with Is Trigger ticked,
  • the Hazard script, with Bounce Speed at 5.

The kinematic body moves only where code puts it and ignores gravity. The trigger plus Hazard means touching the drone costs a heart, and the invulnerability window in Health stops it from draining you while it hovers over you.

Create an empty object called Route_Teach (not a child of the drone) and give it three or four empty children placed across the open room: P0, P1, P2. Click the cube icon at the top left of the Inspector for each to give it a colored label you can see in the Scene view.

Now the first version of the brain, which only patrols. Add EnemyAI to the drone:

Lock the Inspector (the padlock icon at its top right) while the drone is selected, then drag P0, P1, and P2 onto Waypoints. Press Play. The drone loops the route at a steady 2 units per second. Click the padlock again when you're done.

#Step 4: Senses, Chase, and Search

Replace the script with the full version. It keeps the patrol and adds the state machine from the Notes lesson, plus a Setup method the spawner will use:

Fill the new slots: Player from the Hierarchy, Sight Blockers set to Ground only, Sprite from the drone's own Sprite Renderer, and an alert beep from sfxr.me. All state changes go through SetState, so the color, the sound, and the search timer can never get out of step with the state itself.

Look at what Search does with lastSeen. It's the player's position on the last physics step when the drone could still see them, so the straight line from the drone to that point was clear a moment ago. Search follows a path the drone knows is open.

Press Play and test each arrow of the diagram:

⚠️ Watch out

A kinematic drone flies through tiles. While it chases or searches it follows lines it could see along, but its trip back to the route after a search is a straight line that can pass through a thin wall. This build handles that with level design: each drone gets an open room, as the Notes lesson suggested. Pathfinding is the code fix, and it's a much bigger job.

#Step 5: Make it a prefab, then build the spawner

Drag the drone into Prefabs. Open the prefab and notice that Player is now empty and refuses the scene's Player. That's expected: prefabs can't reference scene objects. Drones you place by hand keep their scene references as overrides, and spawned drones get theirs from the spawner.

Create an empty Spawner object in the twist room, give it two empty children as spawn points near the ceiling, and make a Route_Twist with waypoints spread across the room. Add:

A few details matter here. Making Start return IEnumerator turns it into a coroutine, so the whole spawn loop reads top to bottom with a yield where it waits. enemy == null is true for drones Unity has destroyed, so RemoveAll keeps the count honest. Destroy(enemy.gameObject, enemyLifetime) retires each drone after 15 seconds, which keeps a steady stream flowing instead of three drones that hover forever.

Drag the drone prefab (from the Project window this time) into Enemy Prefab, and fill the spawn points, the route, and the Player.

#Step 6: Tune the beats by playing them

Now arrange the slice from the diagram and play it from the start each time you change something:

  • Teach room: set the drone's Detect Radius small (4) and its route high, so a player on the floor is never seen. Put a coin trail along the floor that leads under its path.
  • Test corridor: a hand-placed drone whose route crosses the path at head height, and a pillar of Ground tiles to hide behind. Waiting behind the pillar should be enough to pass.
  • Twist room: the spawner, with spikes on parts of the floor so hiding isn't free. Start with Max Alive at 2 and raise it only if the room feels easy.
  • Exit: a few safe tiles, a last coin, and the exit marker you'll wire up in the capstone.

Ask a friend to play without hints and watch where they hesitate. If they die in the teach room, it isn't teaching yet.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does SetState handle the color, the alert sound, and the search timer, instead of each case doing it?

  • It does; the cases already call Patrol and MoveTowards.

  • If one case forgot to recolor the drone, the player would see white while being chased.

  • It changes nothing about speed; it keeps state and feedback in sync.

Show answer

B. If one case forgot to recolor the drone, the player would see white while being chased.

2Why is the Ground tilemap's collider merged with a Composite Collider 2D?

  • Merging turns hundreds of boxes into one shape per solid area.

  • A Tilemap Collider 2D alone does collide; it's just made of many small boxes.

  • The drone is kinematic and passes through static colliders either way.

Show answer

A. Merging turns hundreds of boxes into one shape per solid area.

3The spawner's alive list keeps references to drones. Why call alive.RemoveAll(enemy => enemy == null) each loop?

  • It doesn't destroy anything; it only forgets drones that are already gone.

  • Without it the list fills with dead entries, alive.Count stays at the cap, and spawning stops for good.

  • Instantiate doesn't know about the list. The cap is your own rule.

Show answer

B. Without it the list fills with dead entries, alive.Count stays at the cap, and spawning stops for good.

Key takeaways

  • Use separate tilemaps for background, solid ground, and hazards; merge the ground's collider with a Composite Collider 2D set to Merge.
  • A kinematic drone with MovePosition gives exact patrols and still fires trigger events against the player.
  • Route every state change through one method so color and sound always match the state.
  • A spawner passes scene references to each copy, caps the count, and cleans up after destroyed enemies.
  • Tune each section by playing it from the start, and watch someone else play it.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a Rule Tile (Create > 2D > Tiles > Rule Tile, from the 2D Tilemap Extras package) so edges and corners pick the right sprite automatically.
  • Add a warning stage before Chase: the drone turns orange and pauses for 0.3 seconds before it moves, which gives the player time to react.
  • Let the player defeat a drone by landing on it, and award points through ScoreKeeper.

#Further reading

  • Tile palettes (opens in a new tab): creating palettes and every painting tool.
  • Physics2D.Linecast (opens in a new tab): the layer mask and depth parameters, and what the returned hit contains.
  • AnimationCurve (opens in a new tab): keys, Evaluate, and the wrap modes that decide what happens past the last key.
