m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Change how an enemy walks its route without touching its other states.
  • Use downward and forward raycasts to keep a ground enemy on its platform.
  • Rearrange a level's sections so each mechanic is taught before it's tested.
  • Add an attack that warns, commits, and recovers, so players can learn to dodge it.
  • Predict how a spawn curve and a cap interact, then build spawning in waves.

#Warm-up: where does the drone go next?

A drone has four waypoints and starts heading for index 0. After it reaches each one it runs index = (index + 1) % 4;. Write down the next eight indexes it heads for, then check:

The route loops, so after waypoint 3 the drone flies straight back to waypoint 0, crossing the whole room. That's fine for a circle-shaped route. For a route along a line, the next exercise is a better fit.

#Exercise 1: Ping-pong patrol

Make the drone go back and forth along its route instead of looping: with four waypoints it should head for 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, and so on. Only the line that advances the index should change.

Need a hint?

Keep a direction that is +1 or -1. Before stepping, check whether the step would leave the array; if it would, flip the direction first.

Show solution

Check the logic in Python first:

The C# version replaces the % line in Patrol:

Call AdvanceWaypoint() where Patrol used to update the index. The guard for fewer than two waypoints stops a one-point route from flipping direction forever.

#Exercise 2: A walker that stays on its platform

Make a ground enemy (a slime, say) that walks left and right, turning around at walls and at the edge of a platform. It uses a Dynamic Rigidbody2D with gravity, and Freeze Rotation Z ticked under Constraints so it doesn't tip over.

Expected behavior:

Need a hint?

Two raycasts each physics step. One points down from a spot just ahead of the feet ("is there floor ahead?"). The other points forward from the center ("is there a wall right in front?"). If there's no floor or there is a wall, flip direction.

Show solution

Set floorProbe a little longer than the distance from the enemy's center to its feet; if it's too short, the ray never reaches the floor and the slime turns every step. Keep its own layer out of groundLayers, or the forward ray starts inside its own collider and always reports a wall. The script only sets the x velocity, so gravity still pulls it down if the player shoves it off a ledge.

#Exercise 3: Fix a level that tests before it teaches

A teammate's level has these sections, left to right. Playtesters keep quitting in section 2.

Rewrite the order (you may add or change sections) so each mechanic gets taught, tested, and then combined, and say what each section is for.

Need a hint?

List the mechanics first: spikes, drones, and the combination. Each needs its own safe introduction before the combination can be fair. Where would you put a checkpoint?

Show solution
# Section Purpose
1 Short run with a coin trail Warm up the controls
2 One spike pit with an easy jump Teach spikes where failure is cheap (it was section 3)
3 Two pits with a shorter landing Test spikes
4 Drone patrolling an empty room, seen from a ledge first Teach drones (it was section 4)
5 Drone route crossing the path, pillar for cover Test drones
6 Checkpoint and a quiet stretch Rest before the hard part
7 Wide shaft with spikes and one drone Twist: the combination, now fair (it was section 2)
8 Easy run to the exit Conclude

The original section 2 wasn't a bad idea, just early: it combined two mechanics the player hadn't met yet. Widening the shaft in its new position also leaves room to dodge, which a narrow shaft didn't.

#Exercise 4: An attack that warns, commits, and recovers

Add three states after Chase. Within 2.5 units, the drone stops and glows orange for 0.5 seconds (Windup). Then it dashes 4 units in a straight line toward where the player was when the wind-up ended (Dash, 0.35 seconds, speed 9). Then it drifts slowly for 1 second (Cooldown) before returning to Chase.

Need a hint?

Each timed state needs an end time. Set it in SetState when the state begins, and in the case, compare Time.time against it. Lock the dash target at the moment Windup ends; if the dash kept tracking the player, nobody could dodge it.

Show solution

And at the top of SetState:

Add an orange case to the color choice for Windup. This three-part shape (a warning the player can read, a committed action, and a window of safety afterward) is how most action games make attacks feel fair.

#Exercise 5: Predict the pacing

The spawner from the build uses a curve that falls linearly from 6 seconds to 2 seconds over the first 120 seconds, then stays at 2. Before running anything, guess how many drones spawn in each 30-second block of a 3-minute run. Then work out when Max Alive = 3 with a 15-second lifetime starts to be the real limit.

Need a hint?

Simulate it: start at time 0, spawn, add the current interval, repeat. For the cap, think about how many drones are alive at once if a new one arrives every interval seconds and each lives 15.

Show solution

Spawn attempts climb from 6 in the first block to 15 in each of the last two. But with a 15-second lifetime, about 15 ÷ interval drones are alive at once, which reaches 3 when the interval drops to 5 seconds, 30 seconds in. After that the cap, not the curve, sets the pressure: attempts beyond it are skipped. If the late game feels flat, raise the cap over time instead of shortening the interval further.

#Exercise 6: Spawn in waves

Replace the endless spawner in the twist room with three waves: 2 drones, then 3, then 5. Each wave starts 3 seconds after the previous wave is completely gone. A HUD label shows Wave 2/3, and at the end it shows All waves cleared.

Need a hint?

A [System.Serializable] class with count and spacing fields shows up as an editable list in the Inspector. yield return new WaitUntil(() => condition) waits until the condition is true. The drones need a way to disappear, so keep the lifetime from the build.

Show solution

Fill the Waves list in the Inspector with counts 2, 3, and 5. Cycling spawn points with i % spawnPoints.Length spreads each wave out instead of stacking drones on one spot. Once you let the player defeat drones, the waves end sooner for players who fight, which rewards skill without any extra code.

#Challenge: Raise the alarm

When a drone switches to Chase, every other drone within 8 units should switch to Search, heading for the player's current position, even if it can't see the player itself. Drones that are already chasing ignore the alarm.

Need a hint?

Put drones on an Enemy layer. In SetState, when entering Chase, call Physics2D.OverlapCircleAll(rb.position, 8f, enemyLayers), get each collider's EnemyAI, skip this, and call a new public Alert(Vector2 position) method that sets lastSeen and enters Search only if the drone isn't already chasing. Check for alarm loops: if Alert could trigger Chase, one drone would alert the next forever.

What you'll learn

  • Decide which data belongs in PlayerPrefs and which belongs in a JSON save file.
  • Save and load a [Serializable] class with JsonUtility, File, and Application.persistentDataPath.
  • List the ways a build differs from Play mode in the Editor, and test for each one.
  • Run a playtest that produces evidence instead of opinions.
  • Find the slow part of a frame with the Profiler's CPU Usage module.
  • Set up a Web build in File > Build Profiles and know what itch.io needs from it.

Your friend plays to the third checkpoint on Friday. On Monday they open the game again and it starts at the beginning, score 0. Nothing crashed, nothing was "wrong," and they still won't play a fourth time. A game that forgets is a game that feels unfinished.

The same weekend, you send them a build. In the Editor the Restart button works; in the build it does nothing, because the scene was never added to the build's scene list. The Editor quietly forgives things a build won't, and this module is about closing both gaps.

#Decide what to save before deciding how

Not everything needs saving, and the right storage depends on what the data is:

Data Example Store it in
Settings Volume, "reduce flashing" PlayerPrefs
A single record Best score, best time PlayerPrefs
Progress Level, checkpoint, score, health, coins collected A JSON save file
Things you can rebuild Where each drone was mid-patrol Nothing; reset them on load

That last row is a design decision as much as a technical one. Saving at checkpoints and restoring "you're at checkpoint 2 with 340 points" is far simpler than freezing every object, and players expect it.

#PlayerPrefs: a tiny key-value store

PlayerPrefs stores ints, floats, and strings under string keys, and it survives quitting the game:

The second argument of GetInt is the default for a key that doesn't exist, so the first run needs no special case. PlayerPrefs.Save() writes to disk now instead of waiting for the game to quit, which matters if the game crashes or the browser tab closes.

Where the data goes depends on the platform: the registry on Windows, a .plist file on macOS, and the browser's IndexedDB storage (up to 1 MB) in a Web build. It isn't encrypted, so a curious player can edit it. Keep it to small values you wouldn't mind someone changing.

#JSON save files with JsonUtility

For progress, write a plain C# class with the fields you need and mark it [Serializable]:

JsonUtility.ToJson turns an instance into text, and File.WriteAllText writes that text to a file in a folder Unity guarantees is writable:

With prettyPrint set to true, the file is readable, which helps a lot when debugging:

JsonUtility is fast and built in, but strict about what it will serialize:

  • The class needs [Serializable], and so does any class you nest inside it.
  • Only fields are saved: public ones, or private ones marked [SerializeField]. Properties such as public int Score { get; set; } are skipped.
  • List<T> and arrays of serializable types work as fields. Dictionary doesn't, and the top-level value must be an object, not a bare array.

One behavior works in your favor. When FromJson reads a file that's missing a field, that field keeps the value from its initializer. Add public float bestTime = 0f; next month, and old save files still load, with bestTime at 0. The version field lets you detect old files when you need to convert them.

Application.persistentDataPath is a different folder on each platform. On Windows it's usually %userprofile%\AppData\LocalLow\<company>\<product>, and on macOS it's ~/Library/Application Support/<company>/<product>. Print it once with Debug.Log(Application.persistentDataPath) so you can find and delete the file while testing.

#A build is not Play mode

The Editor is generous. A build is literal. Before you send a build to anyone, check the differences that bite most often:

  • Only listed scenes exist. A scene that isn't in the build's Scene List can't be loaded, and SceneManager.LoadScene logs an error instead.
  • There's no Console window. In a desktop build, Debug.Log output and errors go to a log file; in a Web build, they go to the browser's developer console (open it with F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac). Test with a Development Build, which adds debug information and can connect to the Profiler, before your final build.
  • The frame rate changes. A build may run at 60, 144, or 30 frames per second. Anything that moves without Time.deltaTime (or outside FixedUpdate) changes speed.
  • The screen changes. A browser window or a laptop screen is a different size and shape from your Game view, which is what the Canvas Scaler settings from Module 5 are for.
  • Startup order can change. If one script reads another's data in Awake, it may work in the Editor by luck. Set up your own state in Awake, and read other objects in Start.
  • Web builds have browser rules. The page must be served by a web server, so double-clicking index.html doesn't work. Browsers keep audio silent until the player clicks or presses a key, and the keyboard only reaches the game after the player clicks on it.

#Playtesting: watch, don't explain

You can't see your own game fresh. Someone who has never played it can, but only if you stay quiet. A playtest that produces useful evidence goes like this:

  1. Give one sentence of setup ("It's a platformer; arrow keys and space"), then stop talking.
  2. Ask them to think out loud: what they're trying to do and what they expect.
  3. Write down every hesitation, death, and "wait, what?" along with the section it happened in. Count deaths per section.
  4. Don't help. If they're stuck for two minutes, note it, then help and carry on.
  5. Afterward, ask three questions: "What was hardest?", "When were you confused?", and "What did the drones do?"

Fix the top three problems, then test with a different person. If you can, log events from the game with Debug.Log (a checkpoint reached, a death and where it happened), and count them afterward instead of relying on memory.

#The Profiler: measure before you optimize

At 60 frames per second each frame has 16.7 milliseconds. When the game stutters, something is taking longer, and guessing what is usually wrong. Open Window > Analysis > Profiler, press Play, and let it record. The CPU Usage chart at the top shows each frame's time. Click a tall spike, switch the lower panel to Hierarchy, and sort by Total time, or by GC Alloc to find code that creates garbage.

Here's a script that shows up badly:

FindFirstObjectByType searches every object in the scene, and Unity's documentation warns against calling it every frame. The string concatenation allocates memory each frame, and the garbage collector eventually pauses the game to clean it up. The fix is what you already did in Module 5: keep a reference set in the Inspector, and change the text only when the Changed event fires.

Profiling in the Editor includes the Editor's own overhead, so the numbers run high. For real figures, make a Development Build with Autoconnect Profiler ticked, and the Profiler attaches to the running build.

#Build Profiles and the Web platform

Unity 6 replaced the old Build Settings window with File > Build Profiles. The left side lists Platforms such as Windows, macOS, Linux, and Web, and you can also create your own profiles. Each platform has a Scene List: the scenes included in the build, in order, with the first one loading at startup. Add Open Scenes adds what you have open, and dragging reorders.

To make a Web build, select Web. If its module isn't installed, add Web Build Support to your Editor from Unity Hub. Switch the active platform to Web, set the scene list, and click Build, choosing an empty folder outside Assets. You get an index.html and the files it loads. Settings that change how the page loads, such as Compression Format and Decompression Fallback, live in Edit > Project Settings > Player under the Web tab's Publishing Settings.

That folder is what itch.io hosts. Zip its contents, upload the zip as an HTML project, and itch.io plays it in the page. The build-along walks through every click.

⚠️ Watch out

The save file says {}. If SaveData uses properties (public int Score { get; set; }) or is missing [Serializable], JsonUtility.ToJson writes an empty object without any error, and loading gives you defaults. Use public fields, or private fields with [SerializeField], and open the file to check it.

⚠️ Watch out

Web saves on itch.io and new uploads. itch.io serves each new upload from a different path, and browser storage is tied to the path, so uploading a new build can reset players' saves. Tell players in your update notes, and test saving in the uploaded build itself.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Where should the music volume setting and the player's current checkpoint be stored?

  • Volume is one small setting; the checkpoint belongs with the rest of the progress data.

  • It would work for two values, but progress grows (coins, levels, health) and is easier to manage as one file.

  • Then "New Game," which deletes the save, would also reset the player's volume.

Show answer

A. Volume is one small setting; the checkpoint belongs with the rest of the progress data.

2SaveData has public int Score { get; set; } and [Serializable]. What does JsonUtility.ToJson(data) produce?

  • That's what a library that reads properties would produce. JsonUtility serializes fields only.

  • The property's hidden backing field isn't serialized, so nothing is written, and no error is shown.

  • There's no error at all, which is why this bug is easy to miss.

Show answer

B. The property's hidden backing field isn't serialized, so nothing is written, and no error is shown.

3You double-click index.html in your Web build folder and the game doesn't load. What's the problem?

  • The files are fine; the way they were opened is the problem.

  • Use Build and Run, which starts a local server, or upload to itch.io.

  • They run in current versions of the major desktop browsers.

Show answer

B. Use Build and Run, which starts a local server, or upload to itch.io.

4The Profiler shows ScoreLabel.Update allocating memory every frame, and the game stutters every few seconds. What's the most likely cause?

  • The size of the number doesn't matter.

  • Updating the text only when the score changes removes almost all of that garbage.

  • It can, but rebuilding text every frame for no reason is wasted work.

Show answer

B. Updating the text only when the score changes removes almost all of that garbage.

Key takeaways

  • Settings and single records go in PlayerPrefs; progress goes in a [Serializable] class written as JSON.
  • JsonUtility saves fields, not properties; missing fields keep their initializer values, which makes adding fields safe.
  • Save under Application.persistentDataPath, and print the path so you can find the file.
  • Test a Development Build before shipping: scene list, frame rate, screen size, startup order, and browser rules.
  • Playtest in silence, count where people struggle, and measure with the Profiler before optimizing.

#Further reading

  • JSON serialization (opens in a new tab): exactly what JsonUtility supports, FromJsonOverwrite, and how it compares to other serializers.
  • Unity Profiler (opens in a new tab): every module and view, and how to profile a running build.
  • Build Profiles (opens in a new tab): platforms, custom profiles, and which settings they share.

What you'll learn

  • Build a SaveSystem that writes JSON to a file on desktop and to PlayerPrefs in Web builds.
  • Save at checkpoint triggers and restore position, score, and health when the scene loads.
  • Store a volume setting with PlayerPrefs and apply it at startup.
  • Test the save in every situation that breaks saves: first run, reload, damaged file, deleted file.
  • Make a Web build with File > Build Profiles, test it locally, and publish it on itch.io for free.

At the end of this build, anyone with the link can play your game in a browser. Touch a checkpoint flag and a "Saved" message appears; close the tab, come back tomorrow, and you start at that flag with your score and health intact. The volume slider remembers where you left it.

#Step 1: The save data and a save system with two backends

Create SaveData.cs with the class from the Notes lesson (version, scene name, checkpoint id, score, health). Then the save system. Desktop builds write a file. Web builds store the same JSON text in PlayerPrefs instead, because browser file storage doesn't always flush right away, while PlayerPrefs.Save() writes to the browser's storage when you call it.

The #if lines are compiler directives: the compiler keeps only one branch, depending on the platform you build for. UNITY_WEBGL is the symbol Unity defines for Web builds, and !UNITY_EDITOR keeps the file version while you test in the Editor. TryLoad returns false instead of crashing when there's no save or the text isn't valid JSON (FromJson throws an ArgumentException for that), so the game simply starts fresh.

#Step 2: Restore methods on the scripts that own the data

ScoreKeeper and Health own their values, so they get the methods that set them. Add one method to each:

Both raise their events, so the HUD updates on its own. Restore clamps to at least 1 so a save made at 0 health can never load a dead player.

#Step 3: Checkpoints that save, with feedback

Make a checkpoint from a flag sprite with a Box Collider 2D set to Is Trigger, and add:

Place one before the test corridor (cp1) and one before the twist room (cp2) from Module 6. Give each a different Id.

Players should see that saving happened. Add a TextMeshPro text saying "Saved" near the bottom of the HUD and this script on the HUD:

Saved is static because there are several checkpoints and the toast doesn't care which one fired.

#Step 4: Load on startup

Add this to GameSystems, then drag in the Player, its Health, and both checkpoints:

The Restart button from Module 5 reloads the scene, so dying now sends the player back to the last checkpoint instead of the start. [ContextMenu] adds Delete save to the menu that opens when you right-click the component's header in the Inspector, which saves you from hunting for the file while you test.

#Step 5: A volume setting that sticks

Put a UI > Slider in your pause panel (or a corner of the HUD), set Min Value 0 and Max Value 1, and add:

AudioListener.volume scales every sound in the game. SetValueWithoutNotify moves the slider to the saved value without firing onValueChanged, so loading doesn't immediately write the value back. The setting lives apart from the progress save, so deleting the save never resets the volume.

#Step 6: Try to break the save

Run each test in the Editor and note the result. Use Delete save between tests.

Find save.json by logging Application.persistentDataPath once and opening that folder.

#Step 7: Make a Web build

  1. Open File > Build Profiles and select Web under Platforms. If Unity says the module isn't installed, add Web Build Support to this Editor version in Unity Hub (Installs, then the Editor's options menu, then Add modules) and reopen the project.
  2. Make Web the active platform with the Switch Platform button. The first switch reimports assets and can take several minutes.
  3. In the Scene List, make sure your level is listed and ticked. Use Add Open Scenes if it isn't.
  4. Open Edit > Project Settings > Player. Set Company Name and Product Name (the product name is the page title). On the Web tab, under Resolution and Presentation, note the Default Canvas Width and Height (960 × 600 is typical); itch.io will need the same numbers.
  5. Back in Build Profiles, click Build and Run and choose a new, empty folder outside Assets, such as Builds/Web next to the Assets folder. Unity builds, starts a small local web server, and opens the game in your browser.

Play the build through from the start. Click inside the game first so it receives the keyboard. Then run the save tests again in this build: saves here go to browser storage, not to save.json.

The folder now holds index.html, a Build folder, and a TemplateData folder.

#Step 8: Publish it on itch.io

itch.io's terms say accounts are for people 13 and older, and that publishers must be 18 or have a parent's or guardian's consent. If that's not you yet, publish together with a parent or guardian on their account.

  1. Open Builds/Web, select the contents (index.html, Build, TemplateData), and compress them into a zip. On Windows, right-click and choose Compress to ZIP file (or Send to > Compressed (zipped) folder); on a Mac, right-click and choose Compress 3 Items. Zipping the contents, not the folder around them, puts index.html at the top level of the zip.
  2. On itch.io, open your dashboard and create a new project. Give it a title, and set the kind of project to HTML.
  3. Upload the zip and tick the option that says the file will be played in the browser.
  4. Under the embed options, set the viewport to your canvas size (960 × 600) and turn on the fullscreen button. Leave "mobile friendly" off for a keyboard game.
  5. Set pricing to no payments (or "$0 or donate" if you'd like tips), and keep visibility on Draft.
  6. Save, view the page, and play the whole game there. Check the save one more time.
  7. When it works, change visibility to Public. A newly published page appears in itch.io's "most recent" listings once, so polish the page before you publish.

If the game loads forever on itch.io, the browser couldn't decompress the files. Tick Decompression Fallback in Player > Web > Publishing Settings, rebuild, and upload the new zip.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does SaveSystem use PlayerPrefs in Web builds instead of writing save.json?

  • They can; the JSON text is exactly the same on every platform.

  • The data is the same JSON either way; only where it's kept changes.

  • It isn't encrypted on any platform.

Show answer

B. The data is the same JSON either way; only where it's kept changes.

2Why should the build go into a folder outside Assets?

  • You'd get duplicate files, slow imports, and possibly a build that includes the previous build.

  • Any folder outside Assets works.

  • itch.io never sees where the folder was; the problem is Unity importing the build.

Show answer

A. You'd get duplicate files, slow imports, and possibly a build that includes the previous build.

3A friend says the game on itch.io ignores the arrow keys, but the mouse works. What's the first thing to check?

  • It is, or the game wouldn't compile. Input works once the game has focus.

  • Browsers send key presses to whatever part of the page has focus.

  • The size affects layout, not which element receives keys.

Show answer

B. Browsers send key presses to whatever part of the page has focus.

Key takeaways

  • Hide where saves live behind one SaveSystem, so the rest of the game just calls Save and TryLoad.
  • Treat a missing or damaged save as "start fresh," never as a crash.
  • Let the scripts that own data (ScoreKeeper, Health) restore it, so their events keep the HUD in sync.
  • Keep settings separate from progress, so starting a new game doesn't reset them.
  • Test the build itself, locally with Build and Run and again on itch.io as a draft, before making it public.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a title scene with Continue (enabled only when TryLoad succeeds) and New Game (which calls SaveSystem.Delete()).
  • Save the "Reduce flashing" and "Captions" options from Module 5's challenge. PlayerPrefs has no Bool type, so store them with PlayerPrefs.SetInt(key, value ? 1 : 0).
  • Make a Windows, macOS, or Linux build too, and upload it to the same itch.io page as a download.

#Further reading

  • Deploy a Web application (opens in a new tab): compression, server headers, and what Decompression Fallback does.
  • itch.io: uploading HTML5 games (opens in a new tab): the zip rules, file limits, and every embed option.
  • PlayerPrefs (opens in a new tab): where the data is stored on each platform and the size limit on the Web.

What you'll learn

  • Predict exactly what JsonUtility writes for a given class.
  • Find and fix data that a save silently loses.
  • Give scene objects stable IDs and restore their state from a save.
  • Load old save files after the save format changes.
  • Remove per-frame allocations that the Profiler points to.

#Warm-up: predict the JSON

Using the SaveData class from this module (fields version = 1, sceneName = "Level1", checkpointId = "", score, and health = 5), what does this log?

Decide before reading on. Every field is written, including the ones you didn't set, which keep their initializer values. With prettyPrint left at false, it's all on one line:

#Exercise 1: A best score that only goes up

When the player reaches the exit, compare the score with the best score in PlayerPrefs. If it's higher, store it and show New best: 450; otherwise show Best: 520.

Need a hint?

PlayerPrefs.GetInt(key, 0) returns 0 the first time, so any score beats it. Call PlayerPrefs.Save() after setting, in case the browser tab closes right away.

Show solution

Call Submit(ScoreKeeper.Instance.Score) from your exit trigger. A best score is a single record that should survive "New Game," which is why it lives in PlayerPrefs and not in the progress save.

#Exercise 2: Where did the stats go?

A teammate added stats to the save. The game saves without errors, but after loading, jumps and deaths are always 0. This is the code and the file it wrote:

Explain what's missing and fix it.

Need a hint?

Look at which classes have an attribute above them. JsonUtility decides what to write separately for each nested class.

Show solution

PlayerStats has no [Serializable] attribute, so Unity's serializer treats the stats field as something it can't save and skips it, without an error. Add the attribute:

Now the file contains "stats":{"jumps":12,"deaths":3}. Whenever a save seems to lose data, open the file before debugging the loading code: if the data isn't in the file, the bug is in saving.

#Exercise 3: Remember which coins were collected

Right now, reloading at a checkpoint brings back every coin, so a player can farm points. Save the IDs of collected coins, and on load, remove those coins from the level. Coins collected after the last checkpoint should come back, since that progress wasn't saved.

Need a hint?

Each coin needs an ID that is the same every time the scene loads. A field set by Reset() is shared by every instance of a prefab, so it doesn't work. A coin that never moves can build its ID from the scene name and its position. Keep the collected IDs in a static HashSet<string>, and load it in Awake, which runs before any coin's Start.

Show solution

Add public List<string> collectedCoins = new List<string>(); to SaveData (with using System.Collections.Generic;). Then a small shared set:

In Coin:

In Checkpoint, when building the SaveData, add collectedCoins = new List<string>(CoinTracker.Collected). In SaveLoader, load the set in Awake:

Awake matters: Unity runs every Awake before any Start, so the set is ready before coins check it. Clearing first also throws away coins grabbed after the last checkpoint, which then reappear. The cost of position-based IDs is that moving a coin in the Editor gives it a new ID, so old saves won't recognize it.

#Exercise 4: Load saves from an older version

Version 1 of your game saved the checkpoint as a number, "checkpoint": 2. Version 2 uses string IDs like "cp2". Players have version 1 saves. Make version 2 load them correctly.

Need a hint?

Keep the old field in the class so JsonUtility still reads it, with a default that means "not present." Fields missing from a file keep their initializer values. After loading, check version.

Show solution

In SaveSystem.TryLoad, after FromJson succeeds:

A version 1 file contains "version":1, so the check runs; a version 2 file doesn't contain checkpoint, so it stays -1 and is ignored. The next save writes a clean version 2 file. Bumping version whenever the format changes is what makes this possible, so include it from the first release.

#Exercise 5: Fix what the Profiler found

The Profiler's Hierarchy view, sorted by GC Alloc, puts this script at the top every frame, and the frame time spikes every few seconds:

Name four costs, and rewrite it so nothing allocates per frame.

Need a hint?

Ask of each line: does it search, create something new, or do I/O, every frame? Then ask whether the value it computes changes every frame at all.

Show solution

The four costs: FindGameObjectsWithTag searches the scene and allocates a new array every frame; the string concatenation creates a new string every frame; GetComponent runs once per enemy per frame; and Debug.Log every frame is slow and also allocates. The count only changes when an enemy appears or disappears, so make the enemies report that:

TextMeshPro's SetText with a {0} placeholder formats the number without creating a new string. The pulsing color moves into EnemyAI itself, which already has its SpriteRenderer in a field. Profile again and EnemyCounter disappears from the GC Alloc list.

#Exercise 6: Turn a playtest into a decision

You logged events during three playtests with Debug.Log($"PLAYTEST {Time.time:F1} {eventName} {section}") and copied the lines out of the Console. Count deaths per section and how many testers reached each checkpoint, then decide which section to change first.

Need a hint?

Split each line on spaces. Testers are separated by start lines. Count death lines by section, and count checkpoint lines by name.

Show solution

The test corridor causes 7 of the 10 deaths and the only quit, and one tester never got past it. That's the section to fix first, even though the twist room is meant to be harder. Make the pillar wider, or slow the drone there from 2 to 1.5, then test again with someone new and compare the counts.

#Challenge: Three save slots

Let the player choose one of three save slots from a menu. Each slot button shows what's in it, like Slot 2: cp2, 340 points, saved 14 Nov 18:05, or Slot 3: empty.

Need a hint?

Give SaveSystem a slot parameter and build the file name (or PlayerPrefs key) from it, such as save1.json. JsonUtility can't serialize DateTime, so store the time as a string with DateTime.Now.ToString("o") and read it back with DateTime.Parse. Remember which slot is active with a static field, or in PlayerPrefs if it should survive a restart.

What you'll learn

  • Check your idea against the capstone requirements before you start building.
  • Choose a project at the right difficulty and describe it in one sentence and one loop.
  • Cut scope with a Must / Should / Could list until the Musts fit comfortably in your time.
  • Write a one-page design document that answers the questions you'd otherwise answer by accident.

Most first games don't fail because of a bug. They fail because of their size. "An open-world RPG with crafting and multiplayer" never ships. "A platformer where you dodge drones to collect five keys, across three short levels" does, and a finished small game teaches you more, and impresses people more, than half of a big one.

This module is your own game, built with everything from Modules 2 to 7. Here you choose it and plan it. The next lesson builds it in milestones, and the last one tests, polishes, and presents it.

Pick one, or use one as a template for your own. "New" is what you'd learn beyond the course.

Idea Difficulty Core mechanic New
Coin Run: collect 20 coins across two levels to open the exit, dodging patrol drones; best time saved Steady Platforming and timing Almost nothing, so you can spend the time on polish
Lantern Keep: a top-down stealth escape where guards with vision cones patrol and keys open doors Standard Avoid being seen Top-down movement (gravity scale 0), doors and keys
Sky Courier: climb forever on platforms that spawn above you while the floor rises; best height saved Standard Climb under pressure Spawning and cleaning up level chunks
Arena Survivor: survive five waves of enemies, choosing one upgrade between waves; unlocked upgrades saved Stretch Fight and choose Upgrade UI, enemies the player can defeat
Grapple Ruins: a small explorable map where a dash ability, found halfway through, opens new areas; three save slots Stretch Explore and unlock Ability gating, a map that loops back on itself

If you're unsure, choose one level easier than you think you can manage. Finishing early leaves time for polish, which is what makes a game feel good. Finishing late leaves nothing.

#Shrink it until it looks too small

Start with two sentences. The pitch says what the player does and why it's interesting: "Dodge sentry drones to grab five keys before the reactor melts down." The core loop is the set of verbs the player repeats every few seconds:

Then sort every feature you can imagine into three lists:

  • Must: the game isn't a game without it. This should be short.
  • Should: makes it clearly better, and you'll do it if Musts are done.
  • Could: nice ideas you're happy to drop.

Now estimate the hours for each Must and double the total, because everyone underestimates. If the doubled total doesn't fit in your time with room to spare, move Musts down until it does. This feels painful and is the most important planning step.

#The one-page design document

A design doc isn't paperwork. It's the list of decisions you'd otherwise make by accident at 11 p.m. Copy this template into a file called DESIGN.md in your project folder and fill it in. Keep it to one page.

The Levels line is where Module 6 pays off. Write each level as a sentence like "Level 1 teaches jumping over spikes, tests it with gaps, and twists it with a drone over the last gap." If you can't write that sentence, the level isn't designed yet.

#Four milestones

Plan your time as four milestones. Each has a definition of done, so "almost finished" can't hide.

The vertical slice is the most useful milestone. It's one small piece of the game at finished quality, and it tells you early whether the game is fun and how long a level really takes to build. If the slice took three times longer than you planned, cut levels now, not the night before the deadline.

#Art, sound, and credits you're allowed to use

You don't need to draw or compose anything, but every asset needs a license that lets you use it. Good free sources:

  • Kenney (opens in a new tab): thousands of sprites, tiles, UI pieces, and sounds, all CC0 (no credit required).
  • OpenGameArt (opens in a new tab): sprites and music under several licenses. Check each one; CC-BY means you must credit the author.
  • Freesound (opens in a new tab): sound effects, many CC0 or CC-BY. Filter by license when you search.
  • sfxr.me (opens in a new tab) and BeepBox (opens in a new tab): make your own effects and chiptune music in the browser.

Add a credits line for every asset you didn't make, even CC0 ones, to your design doc and, later, to your itch.io page. If you use AI-generated art or sound, itch.io's quality guidelines ask you to say so clearly in the project description.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your Must list adds up to 20 hours of estimates, and you have 30 hours in total. What should you do?

  • Doubled, the estimate is 40 hours, which doesn't fit. Estimates are almost always too low.

  • Doubling corrects for the usual underestimate, and the last milestone needs real time too.

  • The slice is what tells you early that you need to cut, so skipping it makes overruns worse.

Show answer

B. Doubling corrects for the usual underestimate, and the last milestone needs real time too.

2Which of these is a core loop?

  • That's setting. A loop is what the player does every few seconds.

  • These are repeated verbs, and each feeds the next.

  • That's content structure, not the moment-to-moment loop.

Show answer

B. These are repeated verbs, and each feeds the next.

3You found a great sprite pack on OpenGameArt licensed CC-BY 4.0. What do you need to do?

  • Free to download isn't the same as no conditions; CC-BY has one.

  • CC-BY lets you use and change the work as long as you give credit.

  • The license already grants permission, on the condition that you credit the author.

Show answer

B. CC-BY lets you use and change the work as long as you give credit.

Key takeaways

  • Check your idea against the requirements table before you build anything.
  • A pitch and a core loop come first; content comes after the loop is fun.
  • Sort features into Must, Should, and Could, double your estimates, and cut until the Musts fit.
  • A one-page design doc records decisions on purpose, including how each level teaches, tests, and twists.
  • Every milestone has a definition of done, and every asset has a source and a license in your credits.

What you'll learn

  • Set up the scene flow (Title, levels, End) and the build's Scene List in the right order.
  • Run the whole game's flow from one GameManager with Playing, Paused, Won, and Lost states.
  • Carry progress between levels with the save system from Module 7.
  • Build in four milestones, each with a checklist that decides when it's done.
  • Keep a bug list, commit working versions, and stop adding features at the right time.

Your Module 7 project already has most of the systems. What it lacks is a skeleton: a title screen, more than one level, a way to win, and one place that decides whether the game is playing, paused, won, or lost. Build that skeleton first and every milestone after it is "fill in the content."

#Step 1: Folders, scenes, and the Scene List

Keep the project tidy from the start; you'll be in it for a while:

Make the Player and HUD prefabs now, by dragging them from your Module 7 scene into Prefabs. Each level then starts by dragging both in, and a fix to the prefab fixes every level.

Create the four scenes, then open File > Build Profiles and arrange the Scene List in the order shown in the diagram: Title first, because the first scene in the list is the one the build loads at startup, then the levels in play order, then End.

#Step 2: One GameManager for the game's state

The player, enemies, and HUD each have their own little state machines. The game as a whole needs one too. Put this on a GameSystems object in each level (it's a good candidate for a prefab):

Every rule about the game's flow is in one place: Escape only toggles between Playing and Paused, so it can't unpause a Game Over screen, and the time scale always matches the state. Awake resets Time.timeScale to 1 as a safety net, so no scene can ever start frozen because the last one ended paused.

The HUD shows the right panel for each state. It takes the GameManager as an Inspector reference rather than through Instance, so subscribing in OnEnable is safe no matter which object wakes up first:

This replaces the separate GameOverScreen and PauseMenu scripts from Module 5. Point the panels' buttons at GameManager.Resume, Restart, LoadNextLevel, and QuitToTitle.

#Step 3: An exit that saves and moves on

The exit trigger wins the level and saves a "start of the next level" record, so Continue on the title screen picks up there:

On the final level the exit deletes the save instead, so Continue never drops a player onto the End screen. SceneUtility.GetScenePathByBuildIndex turns a Scene List position into a path like Assets/Scenes/Level2.unity, and Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension trims it to Level2. In SaveLoader, only move the player to a checkpoint when data.sceneName matches the current scene; the score is restored either way, so it carries from level to level.

#Step 4: A title screen with Continue and New Game

In the Title scene, add a Canvas with the game's name, two buttons, and this script:

out _ throws away the loaded data when all you need to know is whether a save exists. A greyed-out Continue button tells a first-time player there's nothing to continue, without any text. The End scene needs only a "Thanks for playing" line, the final score, and a button that loads scene 0.

Now check the skeleton by playing the game from the Title scene: New Game, reach the exit, Next, reach the exit, End, back to Title, Continue. Do this from the Title scene at the start of every work session, so you always test the path a real player takes.

#Milestone 1: Grey box

Build every level out of plain shapes (Create > 2D > Sprites > Square gives you a placeholder sprite) and tiles in flat colors. No art, no sound. The question this milestone answers is "is moving through this level interesting?"

Done when:

  • Every level from your design doc exists, start to exit, in grey box.
  • The player can move, jump, and collide everywhere, and the camera follows.
  • The full scene flow works from Title to End.
  • You've written one line per level on what it teaches, tests, and twists.

#Milestone 2: Vertical slice

Pick the first level and make it finished: real art, the Animator, the HUD, sounds, at least one enemy with its state machine, checkpoints, and saving. Leave the other levels in grey box.

Done when:

  • Level 1 looks, sounds, and plays the way you want the whole game to.
  • Someone else has played it while you watched in silence, and you've written down what they struggled with.
  • You've compared the time it took with your estimate, and cut or kept levels based on that.

#Milestone 3: Content complete

Bring every level up to the slice's quality and finish every menu. After this milestone comes the feature freeze: no new mechanics, enemies, or levels, only fixes and polish. Ideas that arrive later go on a "next version" list.

Done when:

  • Every requirement from the capstone table is in the game.
  • Saving works across quitting and reopening, and a damaged save starts fresh.
  • A Development Build runs from Title to End without errors.

#Milestone 4: Ship

Make the Web build, put it on itch.io as a draft, and work through the bug list and the test plan from the next lesson. Make the screenshots and trailer, and publish.

#Keep a bug list and commit when things work

When a playtester or your own testing finds a problem, write it down instead of fixing it immediately, so you fix the worst ones first:

# Bug Steps to reproduce Severity Status
1 Drone flies through the right wall of room 3 Lose it behind the pillar, wait 2 s Medium Fixed: widened room
2 Score resets to 0 when Level 2 starts Finish Level 1, press Next High Open
3 Coin chime is louder than music Grab any coin Low Open

High means a player can't finish or loses progress; fix those first. Low is cosmetic.

Commit (or zip a backup, as Module 1 showed) every time something new works: "Drone patrols level 2," "Continue works." When a change breaks everything at midnight, a commit from an hour earlier turns a disaster into a five-minute rollback.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the Title scene have to be first in the Scene List?

  • It keeps your order; that's why the order matters.

  • Put the levels after it in play order so buildIndex + 1 is always the next level.

  • Any scene can have UI.

Show answer

B. Put the levels after it in play order so buildIndex + 1 is always the next level.

2A playtester can press Escape on the Game Over screen and keep playing with zero health. With this starter's GameManager, why can't that happen?

  • Nothing checks health directly in Update.

  • Keeping every flow rule in one state machine means one place enforces them all.

  • Update still runs at a time scale of 0; only time-based movement and physics stop.

Show answer

B. Keeping every flow rule in one state machine means one place enforces them all.

3After the vertical slice, you realize a level takes about three times longer to build than you planned. What's the best move?

  • The slice just measured your real speed; the plan should change, not you.

  • This is what the vertical slice is for: finding out early while there's still time to adjust.

  • Untested games ship with the bugs that make players quit.

Show answer

B. This is what the vertical slice is for: finding out early while there's still time to adjust.

Key takeaways

  • Build the skeleton (scene flow, GameManager, exit, title) before the content.
  • One game-level state machine owns pause, win, lose, and the time scale.
  • Each milestone ends with a checklist, and the vertical slice is your reality check on scope.
  • After content complete, freeze features and spend the remaining time on fixes and polish.
  • Play from the Title scene every session, track bugs by severity, and commit whenever something works.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a test plan that checks every requirement in both the Editor and the Web build.
  • Run a second playtest round and show, with numbers, that your fixes worked.
  • Polish in the order that matters most to players: readability, then feel, then looks.
  • Capture screenshots and a 30 to 60 second trailer from your own game.
  • Present the game in three minutes and assess it honestly against the rubric.

A game is finished when someone who has never seen it can find it, understand it, play it to the end, and want to tell a friend. Everything here serves that sentence. The code is mostly done; what's left is making sure it works for other people, and showing them why it's worth their time.

#Run a written test plan

"I played it and it seemed fine" isn't a test. Copy this plan into your design doc, add rows for your own mechanics, and fill in both result columns. A row isn't passing until it passes in the Web build, because that's the version players get.

# Area Steps Expected Editor Web build
1 Start Open the game Title screen, music after first click, Continue greyed out on first run
2 Controls Move, jump, and use every action listed on the page Each one works, and the page lists them correctly
3 Collision Walk into every wall type, fall into a pit No passing through walls; falling has a result (damage or respawn)
4 Camera Run the whole of Level 1 Threats appear on screen before they reach you
5 Animation Idle, run, jump, take a hit Each state shows, with no frozen first frame
6 Damage Take hits until you die Bar drops, flash and sound on each hit, Game Over panel at zero
7 Enemy Get spotted, then hide Every state change is visible and audible
8 Pause Escape during play, then Resume Everything stops, including sound, then continues
9 Saving Reach a checkpoint, reload the page or relaunch Resume at that checkpoint with the same score
10 Damaged save Corrupt the save (desktop) or clear site data (Web) Game starts fresh without errors
11 Full run Play from Title to End Every scene loads in order, End returns to Title
12 Screen sizes Try a small browser window and fullscreen HUD stays readable and in its corners

Any failure goes on your bug list with steps to reproduce. Fix the High ones before anything else in this lesson.

#Playtest again, and compare

Run the Module 7 playtest a second time with two or three people who haven't played before. Use the same logging, so you get the same numbers: deaths per section, checkpoints reached, and where anyone quit. Put the old and new counts side by side. "Deaths in the test corridor went from 7 to 2 after widening the pillar" is evidence your design work did something, and it's exactly what the rubric's playtesting row asks for.

#Polish in order of impact

With limited time, polish what players notice most first:

  1. Readability. Can players always tell what's dangerous, what they can stand on, what they can collect, and what just happened? Check contrast between the background and the play layer, and make sure every hit, pickup, and save has feedback.
  2. Feel. Small touches make actions satisfying: a squash of the sprite on landing, a few particles when a coin is collected (Effects > Particle System in the Hierarchy menu), a two-frame hit pause, a short camera shake on damage. Keep each one subtle, and keep flashes to three per second or fewer.
  3. Looks. A consistent art style, a background layer, and a font that matches the mood. Consistency beats detail: one simple style used everywhere looks better than a mix of beautiful and placeholder art.

Stop polishing when the test plan passes and the next fix is cosmetic. Shipping matters more than one more effect.

#Screenshots that sell the game

Screenshots are the first thing people see on itch.io. Take them during real play, at moments with something happening, not menus. Set the Game view to Full HD (1920x1080) from its aspect dropdown, then use a key that saves the frame:

In the Editor, the file appears in your project folder, next to Assets. Take twenty and keep the best three to five: one that shows the core loop clearly, one with an enemy mid-chase, one of a later level, and one of something surprising. Remove the script (or disable it) before your final build.

#A 30 to 60 second trailer

A short gameplay trailer is how most people decide to click. A simple structure that works:

  1. 0 to 5 seconds: gameplay immediately, at its most readable. No logos first.
  2. 5 to 25 seconds: the core loop, one idea per clip, each clip two to four seconds long.
  3. 25 to 45 seconds: escalation, meaning a harder room, more enemies, the twist from each level.
  4. Final 5 seconds: the title, "Play free in your browser," and the itch.io address.

To record, install Recorder from Window > Package Manager (it's in the Unity Registry), open Window > General > Recorder > Recorder Window, choose Add Recorder > Movie, and press Start Recording; it records the Game view in Play mode. OBS Studio (opens in a new tab) is a free alternative that records the Web build in a browser. Play the same section several times and keep your best runs. Cut the clips together in any free video editor and add your game's music.

#The itch.io page

Your page is your game's front door. Before switching from Draft to Public, make sure it has:

  • a cover image (itch.io's editor shows the recommended size) with the title readable at a small size,
  • three to five screenshots and the trailer (itch.io embeds a YouTube link),
  • a short description: the pitch in one sentence, then two or three sentences on what makes it fun,
  • the controls, as a short list,
  • credits for every asset you didn't make, with licenses,
  • a few accurate tags (platformer, pixel art, short), and a note if anything was made with generative AI.

#Present it in three minutes

When you show the game to your class, family, or a club, use a plan so the time goes to the best parts:

Practice once with a timer. Have the game already running with a save at a good checkpoint, so you don't spend the demo on the title screen.

#The rubric

Score your own project honestly before anyone else does. Each row is worth the points shown, for 100 in total.

Area (points) Excellent Solid Needs work
Core requirements (25) Every row of the requirements table works in the Web build One or two rows partly done Several missing or only in the Editor
Code quality (15) Small scripts with one job each, events between systems, no per-frame searches, no errors in the Console Works, with a few long scripts or direct references Errors or warnings during play; hard to change
Feedback (15) Every important event is seen and heard; HUD readable at any size Most events have feedback Players miss hits, pickups, or saves
Level and enemy design (15) Each level teaches, tests, and twists; enemy states are readable and fair Levels are playable but uneven Difficulty spikes or unclear threats
Saving and build (10) Saves survive relaunch, damaged saves start fresh, the Web build runs end to end Saving works with rough edges Saving or the build is broken
Playtesting (10) Two rounds with recorded numbers and changes that improved them One round with notes No playtest evidence
Presentation (10) Complete itch.io page, trailer, screenshots, credits, a timed three-minute demo Page and demo with gaps Missing page or demo

#Reflect, then keep going

Write a short reflection in your design doc while it's fresh. Answer three questions: What took much longer than you expected, and why? Which playtest finding surprised you most? If you started this game again tomorrow, what would you plan differently?

Then decide what's next. Some good directions:

  • Enter a game jam. Jams give you a theme and a deadline (often 48 hours to a week) and a community that plays your game. The itch.io jams calendar (opens in a new tab) lists many that are open to everyone; check each jam's rules and age requirements.
  • Learn the next tools. Unity's Junior Programmer pathway (opens in a new tab) covers 3D, and from there pathfinding (the A* Pathfinding Project or Unity's NavMesh), object pooling with UnityEngine.Pool, ScriptableObject assets for game data, and Input System actions for gamepad support.
  • Ship a second, smaller game. The fastest way to get better is to finish another one, using everything this one taught you about scope.

Key takeaways

  • A feature passes only when it passes in the Web build, so run the test plan there.
  • Repeat the playtest and compare numbers to show your fixes worked.
  • Polish readability first, then feel, then looks, and stop when the next change is cosmetic.
  • Screenshots and a trailer show real gameplay, starting with the clearest moment.
  • Present the game in three timed minutes, score it against the rubric, and write down what you'd plan differently.
